sections.title: Scheme of the Code and Key Definitions (Section 2)
sections.summary: The CPC 1908 is procedural law: 158 sections (the substantive body) and 51 Orders with Rules (First Schedule). Definitions of decree, judgment, order, mesne profits and legal representative are tested year after year, usually in the form of 'which of the following is a decree?'
key_points: STRUCTURE: Part I - Sections 1-158 (the body of the Code: substantive principles such as res judicata, jurisdiction, execution framework, appeals); Part II - Sections 121-158 deal with rules and miscellaneous matters; First Schedule - Orders I to LI with Rules (procedural details which a High Court may amend under Sec 122-125). Sections cannot be altered by the High Court; Orders and Rules can be amended by the High Courts (Sec 122, 129). Where a rule made by a High Court conflicts with the Code, the Code prevails. The Code was substantially amended in 1976, 1999 (Act 46 of 1999) and 2002 (Act 22 of 2002, in force 1 July 2002), and by the Commercial Courts Act 2015 (as amended in 2018) for commercial disputes.

Procedural law is meant to be the handmaid of justice: procedural rules are to be liberally construed; but rules relating to jurisdiction and limitation are strictly applied. Sec 4: savings of special or local laws; Sec 5: application of the Code to revenue courts; Sec 7: Provincial Small Cause Courts; Sec 8: Presidency small cause courts; Sec 3: subordination of courts (District Court subordinate to HC; every civil court of lower grade subordinate to District Court); Sec 6: pecuniary jurisdiction - no court has jurisdiction over suits whose value exceeds its pecuniary limits.

Sec 2(2) DECREE: the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. It shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within Sec 144, but shall not include (a) any adjudication from which an appeal lies as an appeal from an order, or (b) any order of dismissal for default. Explanation: a decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of; it is final when such adjudication completely disposes of the suit; it may be partly preliminary and partly final. ESSENTIALS: (1) an adjudication; (2) in a suit; (3) conclusive determination of rights; (4) formal expression. Types: preliminary (e.g., partition, mortgage, administration, possession with mesne profits - Order 20 Rules 12, 13, 15, 18); final; partly preliminary-partly final; deemed decrees (rejection of plaint; determination of questions under Sec 144; and orders under Order 21 Rules 98 and 100, which Order 21 Rule 103 treats as decrees); ex parte decree; consent decree. A decree can be passed only in a suit, and a decree may be appealed as an appeal from decree (Sec 96). See Shyam Sundar Sarma v Pannalal Jaiswal (2005) on the meaning of 'decree'.

Sec 2(9) JUDGMENT: the statement given by the judge of the grounds of a decree or order. Sec 2(14) ORDER: the formal expression of any decision of a civil court which is not a decree. Difference between decree and order: (a) decree is passed in a suit commenced by presentation of a plaint; an order may be passed in a suit or in any other proceeding (application, execution etc.); (b) a decree conclusively determines the rights of parties on matters in controversy; an order may or may not; (c) a decree may be preliminary or final; an order cannot be preliminary; (d) every decree is appealable unless expressly barred; an order is appealable only if specified in Sec 104 and Order 43 Rule 1; (e) a decree has a judgment; an order may or may not have; (f) a second appeal lies on a decree (Sec 100) but not on an order. Judgment vs decree: a judgment contains reasons; a decree follows the judgment and gives the formal relief (Order 20 Rule 6). Under the Letters Patent, 'judgment' has a wider meaning (Shah Babulal Khimji v Jayaben D. Kania, 1981: an order which affects the merits of the controversy or decides a valuable right of the party - 'intermediary or interlocutory judgments').

Sec 2(12) MESNE PROFITS: those profits which the person in wrongful possession of such property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received therefrom, together with interest on such profits, but shall not include profits due to improvements made by the person in wrongful possession. Mesne profits are awarded as a part of a decree for possession (Order 20 Rule 12): for the period before suit (ascertained or inquiry), and for the period after suit until delivery of possession or relinquishment or three years from the date of the decree, whichever is earlier. Sec 2(11) LEGAL REPRESENTATIVE: a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased and where a party sues or is sued in a representative character the person on whom the estate devolves on the death of the party so suing or sued. Sec 2(10) JUDGMENT-DEBTOR: any person against whom a decree has been passed or an order capable of execution has been made; Sec 2(3) DECREE-HOLDER: any person in whose favour a decree has been passed or an order capable of execution has been made. Sec 2(17) PUBLIC OFFICER: includes a judge, a person in the service or pay of the Government or entrusted with public duties, officer of a court of justice, person authorised to perform any duty in connection with the administration of justice, etc. Sec 2(4) DISTRICT; Sec 2(5) FOREIGN COURT: a court situated outside India and not established or continued by the authority of the Central Government; Sec 2(6) FOREIGN JUDGMENT: the judgment of a foreign court; Sec 2(15) PLEADER.

Related concepts: 'suit' is not defined in the Code - a civil proceeding instituted by the presentation of a plaint (Hansraj Gupta v Dehra Dun-Mussoorie Electric Tramway, 1933 PC). A 'suit of a civil nature': one in which the principal question relates to a civil right (Sec 9 and Explanations). A 'cause of action': the bundle of facts which it is necessary for the plaintiff to prove in order to succeed (Cooke v Gill; Gurdit Singh v Munsha Singh, 1977). A 'plaint' and 'written statement' are pleadings (Order 6 Rule 1). 'Sue' vs 'apply': suits - plaint; applications - petition.

common_traps: Rejection of a plaint IS a decree (deemed); dismissal for default is NOT a decree.
Orders under Order 21 Rules 98 and 100 are treated as decrees (Rule 103); since the 1976 amendment, 'determination of any question within Sec 47' is no longer part of the definition of 'decree'.
A preliminary decree cannot be an 'order'; orders are never preliminary.
Mesne profits exclude profits due to improvements by the wrongdoer; they include interest.

sections.title: Jurisdiction of Civil Courts and Place of Suing (Secs 9, 15-25)
sections.summary: Section 9 (all suits of civil nature), exclusion of jurisdiction, pecuniary/ territorial limits (Secs 15-20), timely objection (Sec 21) and transfer (Secs 22-25). At least one question every year.
key_points: Sec 9: the Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. Explanation I: a suit in which the right to property or to an office is contested is a suit of a civil nature, notwithstanding that such right may depend entirely on the decision of questions as to religious rites or ceremonies. Explanation II: for the purposes of Sec 9, it is immaterial whether or not any fees are attached to the office referred to in Explanation I or whether or not such office is attached to a particular place. A suit of civil nature = one where the principal question relates to determination of civil rights (right to property, contract, tort, status, office); not political or purely religious questions (caste disputes, rights of worship without civil right).

EXPRESS BAR: when a statute expressly ousts the civil court (e.g., Sec 175 MV Act; Sec 34 SARFAESI Act). IMPLIED BAR: when a statute creates a special right/ liability and provides a complete machinery for adjudication. DHULABHAI v STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH (1968): principles - (1) where the statute gives finality to the orders of special tribunals the civil courts' jurisdiction must be held to be excluded if there is adequate remedy to do what the civil courts would normally do in a suit (such a provision, however, does not exclude those cases where the provisions of the particular Act have not been complied with or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure); (2) where there is an express bar of the jurisdiction of the court, an examination of the scheme of the particular Act to find the adequacy or the sufficiency of the remedies provided may be relevant but is not decisive to sustain the jurisdiction of the civil court (where there is no express exclusion the examination of the remedies and the scheme of the particular Act to find out the intendment becomes necessary and the result of the inquiry may be decisive); (3) challenge to the provisions of the particular Act as ultra vires cannot be brought before tribunals constituted under that Act (even the High Court cannot go into that question on a revision or reference from the decision of tribunals); (4) when a provision is already declared unconstitutional or the constitutionality of any provision is to be challenged, a suit is open; (5) questions of the correctness of an assessment apart from its constitutionality are for the decision of the authorities, and a civil suit does not lie if the orders of the authorities are declared to be final or there is an express prohibition in the particular Act; (6) where the particular Act contains no machinery for refund of tax collected in excess of constitutional limits or illegally collected, a suit lies; (7) questions of the correctness of assessment apart from its constitutionality are for the decision of the authorities. Additional: a civil court can look into a case where the tribunal acts without jurisdiction/ in violation of fundamental principles of judicial procedure (Firm of Illuri Subbayya Chetty v State of Andhra Pradesh, 1964).

SUBJECT-MATTER JURISDICTION cannot be conferred by consent, waiver or acquiescence; a decree passed by a court without inherent jurisdiction is a nullity and can be challenged at any stage, even in execution or collateral proceedings (Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan, 1954; Hasham Abbas Sayyad). But objection to territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction may be waived and must be taken at the earliest opportunity (Sec 21). Jurisdiction over parties: Sec 20. Sec 11 CPC read with Sec 9: res judicata. Jurisdiction under Art 226 is not ousted by statutory bars (Whirlpool).

Sec 15: every suit shall be instituted in the court of the lowest grade competent to try it. Sec 16 - SUITS RELATING TO IMMOVABLE PROPERTY: subject to the pecuniary or other limitations prescribed by any law, suits (a) for the recovery of immovable property with or without rent or profits, (b) for the partition of immovable property, (c) for foreclosure, sale or redemption in the case of a mortgage of or charge upon immovable property, (d) for the determination of any other right to or interest in immovable property, (e) for compensation for wrong to immovable property, (f) for the recovery of movable property actually under distraint or attachment, shall be instituted in the court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate. PROVISO: a suit to obtain relief respecting, or compensation for wrong to, immovable property held by or on behalf of the defendant may, where the relief sought can be entirely obtained through his personal obedience, be instituted either in the court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate, or in the court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the defendant actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain (Latin: 'actio in personam' exception based on equity acts in personam - e.g., suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property; suit for injunction restraining a defendant). Sec 17: where a suit is to obtain relief respecting, or compensation for wrong to, immovable property situate within the jurisdiction of different courts, the suit may be instituted in any court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction any portion of the property is situate, provided the entire claim is cognizable by such court as regards the value of the subject-matter. Sec 18: where local limits of jurisdiction of courts are uncertain. Sec 19: SUITS FOR COMPENSATION FOR WRONGS TO PERSON OR MOVABLES: where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within the local limits of the jurisdiction of one court and the defendant resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of another court, the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said courts.

Sec 20 - OTHER SUITS: subject to the limitations aforesaid, every suit shall be instituted in a court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction (a) the defendant, or each of the defendants where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain; or (b) any of the defendants, where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, provided that in such case either the leave of the court is given, or the defendants who do not reside, or carry on business, or personally work for gain, as aforesaid, acquiesce in such institution; or (c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises. Explanation: a corporation shall be deemed to carry on business at its sole or principal office in India or, in respect of any cause of action arising at any place where it has also a subordinate office, at such place. Principles: 'cause of action' - Sec 20(c) requires a material part of the bundle of facts to have arisen within the territory; mere residence of plaintiff is irrelevant (Dhodha House v S.K. Maingi, 2006; Navinchandra N. Majithia v State of Maharashtra, 2000 - Art 226 context). AGREEMENT AS TO JURISDICTION: parties cannot by agreement confer jurisdiction on a court which has none, but where two or more courts have jurisdiction, parties may by agreement choose one and exclude the other (Hakam Singh v Gammon (India) Ltd, 1971; A.B.C. Laminart v A.P. Agencies, 1989 - clauses such as 'subject to Delhi jurisdiction' only ousts other courts if words like 'only', 'exclusive', 'alone' are used or the intention is clear; Swastik Gases v Indian Oil Corporation, 2013 - 'subject to Kolkata jurisdiction' read as exclusive; Patel Roadways v Prasad Trading, 1991 - corporation's cause of action at subordinate office). Choice of forum by agreement is not hit by Sec 28 of the Contract Act.

Sec 21 OBJECTION TO JURISDICTION: (1) no objection as to the place of suing shall be allowed by any appellate or revisional court unless such objection was taken in the court of first instance at the earliest possible opportunity and, in all cases where issues are settled, at or before such settlement, and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice. (2) similar for pecuniary jurisdiction. (3) objection as to competence of the executing court with reference to the local limits of its jurisdiction shall not be allowed by any appellate or revisional court unless taken in the executing court at the earliest possible opportunity and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice. Sec 21A (2002): no suit shall lie challenging the validity of a decree passed in a former suit between the same parties on any ground based on an objection as to the place of suing. Sec 21 does NOT cure inherent lack of jurisdiction (subject matter). Sec 6, Sec 15: pecuniary - courts' limits fixed by State civil courts Acts (Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act 1887; Madras Civil Courts Act, etc.) - valuation of suits: Suits Valuation Act 1887; Court Fees Act 1870.

TRANSFER: Sec 22 - where a suit may be instituted in any one of two or more courts and is instituted in one of such courts, any defendant, after notice to the other parties, may, at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, apply to have the suit transferred to another court, and the court to which the application is made, after considering the objections of the other parties (if any), shall determine in which of the several courts having jurisdiction the suit shall proceed. Sec 23: application to which court - to the appellate court (if the courts are subordinate to the same appellate court) or the High Court (if subordinate to different appellate courts of the same High Court, or to different High Courts). Sec 24: GENERAL POWER OF TRANSFER AND WITHDRAWAL: on the application of any of the parties and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, or of its own motion without such notice, the High Court or the District Court may at any stage (a) transfer any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same; or (b) withdraw any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending in any court subordinate to it, and (i) try or dispose of the same; or (ii) transfer the same for trial or disposal to any court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same; or (iii) re-transfer the same for trial or disposal to the court from which it was withdrawn. A court to which a suit is transferred shall continue the same from the stage at which it was transferred or re-try (Sec 24(3)). Sec 24(5): a suit or proceeding may be transferred under this section although the court from which it is transferred has no jurisdiction to try it. Sec 25: POWER OF THE SUPREME COURT TO TRANSFER SUITS ETC.: on the application of a party and after notice to the parties, the Supreme Court may, at any stage, if satisfied that an order under this section is expedient for the ends of justice, direct that any suit, appeal or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other civil court in one State to a High Court or other civil court in any other State (2002 amendment extended Sec 25 to transfer from one High Court to another or from civil court in one State to another; earlier restricted to State-to-State transfer). Grounds for transfer: convenience of parties, apprehension of bias, balance of convenience, multiplicity, public interest; the discretion is exercised judiciously (Maneka Sanjay Gandhi v Rani Jethmalani, 1979: the plaintiff's convenience is not the sole consideration; a reasonable apprehension of not getting justice).

sections.title: Res Sub Judice (Sec 10), Res Judicata (Sec 11) and Constructive Res Judicata
sections.summary: Perennial favourites: essentials of Secs 10 and 11, Explanations I-VIII, constructive res judicata (Explanation IV), res judicata in different contexts, and the 2026 Supreme Court ruling on interlocutory res judicata.
key_points: Sec 10 STAY OF SUIT (RES SUB JUDICE): no court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, where such suit is pending in the same or any other Court in India having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed, or in any Court beyond the limits of India established or continued by the Central Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court. Explanation: the pendency of a suit in a foreign court does not preclude the courts in India from trying a suit founded on the same cause of action. ESSENTIALS: (1) two suits - one previously instituted, one subsequently instituted; (2) the matter in issue in the subsequent suit must be directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit (the test: whether a decision in the previous suit would operate as res judicata in the subsequent suit - National Institute of Mental Health & Neuro Sciences v C. Parameshwara, 2005); (3) same parties or parties under whom they claim, litigating under the same title; (4) the previously instituted suit is pending in the same or another court competent to grant the relief claimed; (5) the previous suit must be a SUIT - not applications or execution proceedings. Object: to prevent courts of concurrent jurisdiction from simultaneously trying two parallel suits, avoid conflicting decisions and multiplicity. Sec 10 is MANDATORY (the court has no discretion to refuse stay), but it only bars the TRIAL, not the institution of the subsequent suit; the stay applies to the later suit; a decree passed in contravention of Sec 10 is not a nullity (it is an irregularity - Pukhraj D. Jain v G. Gopalakrishna, 2004). Where Sec 10 doesn't strictly apply, the court may stay under its inherent power (Sec 151) in the interest of justice (Indian Bank v Maharashtra State Co-operative Marketing Federation, 1998; Aspi Jal v Khushroo Rustom Dadyburjor, 2013 - Sec 10 applies where the matter in issue is substantially the same; otherwise consolidation or a stay under Sec 151 may be considered).

Sec 11 RES JUDICATA: no court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such court. Maxims: 'nemo debet bis vexari pro una et eadem causa' (no man should be vexed twice for the same cause); 'interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium' (it is in the interest of the State that there be an end to litigation); 'res judicata pro veritate occipitur' (a judicial decision is accepted as correct). Based on public policy (not only on the technicalities of Sec 11; the principle applies even where Sec 11 isn't strictly applicable - e.g., writ petitions (Daryao v State of UP, 1961), industrial disputes, taxation (limited), and between two stages of the same litigation).

ESSENTIALS (conditions) of Sec 11: (1) the matter directly and substantially in issue in the subsequent suit must have been directly and substantially in issue in the former suit; (2) the former suit must have been between the same parties or parties under whom they or any of them claim; (3) the parties must have litigated under the same title; (4) the matter must have been heard and finally decided by the former court; (5) the former court must have been competent to try the subsequent suit or the suit in which the issue is subsequently raised. 'Directly and substantially in issue' = the main point on which the decision turned; contrast 'collaterally or incidentally in issue' (not barred). A 'former suit' means a suit which has been decided prior to the suit in question whether or not it was instituted prior thereto (Explanation I). Competence of the court is determined irrespective of any provisions as to a right of appeal from the decision (Explanation II). The matter must have been alleged by one party and either denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other (Explanation III).

EXPLANATION IV - CONSTRUCTIVE RES JUDICATA: any matter which might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in such former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. Illustration: A sues B for rent for a year and B pleads nothing; a later suit by B contending that rent was not due for want of title is barred - B could and should have taken that ground. Forward Construction Co v Prabhat Mandal (Regd), 1986 - constructive res judicata applies to writ petitions/ interlocutory proceedings and to defences that could have been raised. EXPLANATION V: any relief claimed in the plaint, which is not expressly granted by the decree, shall for the purposes of Sec 11 be deemed to have been refused. EXPLANATION VI: where persons litigate bona fide in respect of a public right or of a private right claimed in common for themselves and others, all persons interested in such right shall, for the purposes of Sec 11, be deemed to claim under the persons so litigating. EXPLANATION VII: the provisions of Sec 11 apply to a proceeding for the execution of a decree and references in this section to any suit, issue or former suit shall be construed as references, respectively, to any proceeding for the execution of the decree, question arising in such proceeding and a former proceeding for the execution of that decree. EXPLANATION VIII: an issue heard and finally decided by a court of limited jurisdiction, competent to decide such issue, shall operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit, notwithstanding that such court of limited jurisdiction was not competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised (added 1976).

SPECIAL ASPECTS: (a) Res judicata applies to ISSUES (decision on issue in an earlier suit binds in a later suit even on a different cause of action - 'issue estoppel'); (b) A DECISION ON A PURE QUESTION OF LAW unconnected with the right of the parties does not operate as res judicata; but where a question of law relates to the right of the parties it does (Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy, 1970; Mohanlal Goenka v Benoy Kishna Mukherjee, 1953: a decision on a jurisdiction question - the principle that a wrong decision on jurisdiction is binding if the court had jurisdiction); (c) A JUDGMENT BY CONSENT/ COMPROMISE decree operates as estoppel between the parties but is not strictly res judicata as nothing is 'heard and decided' (Pulavarthi Venkata Subba Rao v Valluri Jagannadha Rao, 1967: consent decree is in the nature of a contract - but binds); (d) Decisions of appellate courts: where the trial court decides a matter and the appeal is dismissed on a preliminary ground, the trial court's decision on merits still operates as res judicata (Sheodan Singh v Daryao Kunwar, 1966); (e) Interlocutory orders: Satyadhyan Ghosal v Deorajin Debi (1960): the principle of res judicata applies to successive stages of the same proceeding - a matter decided at an earlier stage of the same litigation cannot be reopened at a later stage; (f) Ex parte decrees operate as res judicata; (g) The plea of res judicata must be raised and proved; a party may waive it; (h) Res judicata vs estoppel: res judicata is a bar to the court's jurisdiction to try; estoppel is a rule of evidence; res judicata applies to decisions of competent courts; estoppel arises from the party's conduct; (i) Res judicata and Order 2 Rule 2: Sec 11 relates to a matter decided; Order 2 Rule 2 relates to claims not made in the same cause of action (Gurbux Singh v Bhooralal, 1964).

RECENT (2025-26): (1) The Supreme Court held in July 2025 that res judicata ordinarily cannot be a ground for rejecting a plaint under Order VII Rule 11, since it involves a mixed question of fact and law that must be decided on pleadings and evidence at trial; (2) B.S. LALITHA v BHUVANESH (2026 INSC 499, decided 15 May 2026): the Supreme Court explained INTERLOCUTORY RES JUDICATA - the principle applies between two stages of the same litigation; where an earlier application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC has been decided and attained finality, a second application seeking rejection of the plaint on substantially the same issue is barred; the defendant cannot circumvent the bar by invoking different sub-clauses of Rule 11 in the second application as any such ground could and ought to have been raised in the first application (Explanation IV to Sec 11). The same case dealt with daughters' rights in a partition suit (Sec 6 Hindu Succession Act, as amended in 2005, as a saving clause rather than a jurisdictional bar).

sections.title: Foreign Courts, Foreign Judgments and Foreign States (Secs 13, 14, 44A, 83-87B)
sections.summary: Section 13 grounds and Section 44A (reciprocating territories) are the usual targets.
key_points: Sec 2(5) FOREIGN COURT: a court situated outside India and not established or continued by the authority of the Central Government; Sec 2(6) FOREIGN JUDGMENT: the judgment of a foreign court. Foreign judgment is enforceable in India either by (a) a suit on the judgment (as a debt) or (b) execution under Sec 44A if it is a decree of a superior court of a reciprocating territory.

Sec 13 - WHEN FOREIGN JUDGMENT NOT CONCLUSIVE: a foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title except: (a) where it has not been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction; (b) where it has not been given on the merits of the case; (c) where it appears on the face of the proceedings to be founded on an incorrect view of international law or a refusal to recognise the law of India in cases in which such law is applicable; (d) where the proceedings in which the judgment was obtained are opposed to natural justice; (e) where it has been obtained by fraud; (f) where it sustains a claim founded on a breach of any law in force in India. Mnemonic: C-M-I-N-F-B (Competent court, Merits, International law/ Indian law, Natural justice, Fraud, Breach of Indian law). Sec 13 is a rule of res judicata for foreign judgments; and it applies to judgments, not to the underlying foreign law. A foreign judgment on the merits means that the court applied its mind to the evidence; a decree by default or ex parte without considering evidence is not on merits (International Woollen Mills v Standard Wool (UK) Ltd, 2001: a foreign judgment is 'on the merits' only if the foreign court applied its mind to the merits and not merely on a technical default or without considering the defence).

Competence (Sec 13(a)): the foreign court must be competent both under its own law and in the international sense (the defendant must have submitted to jurisdiction, or been resident/ present in that country, or the cause of action must have arisen there) - R. Viswanathan v Rukn-ul-Mulk Syed Abdul Wajid (1963): a foreign court's jurisdiction in personam requires that the defendant be a subject of, resident in, or have submitted to the jurisdiction of that court; Moloji Nar Singh Rao v Shankar Saran (1962): a decree of a foreign court passed against a defendant who appeared under protest to contest jurisdiction is not a submission. Matrimonial judgments: Y. Narasimha Rao v Y. Venkata Lakshmi (1991): a foreign matrimonial judgment is recognised in India only if the court had jurisdiction under the Act governing the parties, is on a ground available under that Act, and the respondent had submitted to the jurisdiction or consented; residence of a respondent for the purposes of matrimonial jurisdiction.

Sec 14 - PRESUMPTION AS TO FOREIGN JUDGMENTS: the court shall presume, upon the production of any document purporting to be a certified copy of a foreign judgment, that such judgment was pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction, unless the contrary appears on the record; but such presumption may be displaced by proving want of jurisdiction. Sec 44A - EXECUTION OF DECREES PASSED BY COURTS IN RECIPROCATING TERRITORY: (1) where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior courts of any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in India as if it had been passed by the District Court. (2) a certificate from the superior court stating the extent, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted shall be filed along with the decree, and such certificate shall be conclusive proof of the extent of such satisfaction or adjustment. (3) the provisions of Sec 47 shall as from the filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceedings of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of Sec 13. Explanation 1: 'reciprocating territory' means any country or territory outside India which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a reciprocating territory (notified: the United Kingdom, Singapore, Bangladesh, UAE, Malaysia, Trinidad and Tobago, New Zealand, the Cook Islands (including Niue) and the Trust Territories of Western Samoa, Hong Kong, Papua New Guinea, Fiji and Aden); 'superior courts' in relation to any such territory means such courts as may be specified in the said notification. Explanation 2: 'decree' with reference to a superior court means any decree or judgment of such court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty, but shall in no case include an arbitration award, even if such an award is enforceable as a decree or judgment. Decrees of courts of non-reciprocating territories (e.g., USA) cannot be executed directly: a fresh suit must be filed on the foreign judgment (within the limitation period of 3 years from the date of the foreign judgment - Art 101 Limitation Act), and Sec 13 exceptions apply; Alcon Electronics v Celem SA (2017): a foreign decree of a non-reciprocating country can be enforced only by a fresh suit; and in respect of a reciprocating territory, the decree must come under Sec 44A. India has recently been considering the notification of other jurisdictions. The Arbitration Act Part II governs foreign awards (separate regime).

SUITS BY ALIENS AND FOREIGN STATES (Secs 83-87B): Sec 83 - alien enemies residing in India with the permission of the Central Government, and alien friends, may sue in any court otherwise competent to try the suit, as if they were citizens of India; but alien enemies residing in India without such permission, or residing in a foreign country, shall not sue in any such court. Sec 84 - a foreign State may sue in a competent court, provided that the object of the suit is to enforce a private right vested in the Ruler of such State or in any officer of such State in his public capacity. Sec 85 - the Central Government may, at the request of the Ruler of a foreign State, or at the request of any person competent in the opinion of the Central Government to act on behalf of such Ruler, by order, appoint any person to prosecute or defend any suit on behalf of such Ruler. Sec 86 - SUITS AGAINST FOREIGN RULERS, AMBASSADORS AND ENVOYS: (1) no foreign State may be sued in any court otherwise competent to try the suit except with the consent of the Central Government certified in writing by a Secretary to that Government; (2) such consent may be given with respect to a specified suit or to several specified suits or with respect to all suits of any specified class or classes, and may specify, in the case of any suit or class of suits, the court in which the foreign State may be sued, but it shall not be given unless the foreign State has instituted a suit in the court against the person desiring to sue it, or by itself or another, trades within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the court, or is in possession of immovable property situated within those limits and is to be sued with reference to such property or for money charged thereon, or has expressly or impliedly waived the privilege accorded to it by this section; (3) Rulers, Ambassadors and Envoys of foreign States are similarly protected: they may not be arrested or have their property proceeded against in execution except with the consent of the Central Government certified by a Secretary (verify the text of Sec 86(1)-(4)). Sec 87 - style of foreign Rulers as parties to suits. Sec 87A - definitions of 'foreign State' and 'Ruler'. Sec 87B - Secs 85 and 86 apply to the Ruler of a former Indian State (former Indian Rulers). Case: Ethiopian Airlines v Ganesh Narain Saboo (2011): foreign State immunity and commercial transactions; Sec 86 and the restrictive immunity doctrine.

sections.title: Suits by or against the Government and Public Officers (Secs 79-82, Order XXVII)
sections.summary: Section 80 notice (two months), Section 79 (parties), Section 82 (execution against Government) and Order 27 are the frequent questions; the 2025 Supreme Court ruling on non-service of Sec 80 notice is a recent hook.
key_points: Sec 79: in a suit by or against the Government, the authority to be named as plaintiff or defendant shall be (a) in the case of a suit by or against the Central Government, the Union of India; and (b) in the case of a suit by or against a State Government, the State. (See Art 300 of the Constitution.)

Sec 80 - NOTICE: (1) subject to sub-section (2), no suit shall be instituted against the Government (including the Government of the State of Jammu and Kashmir - since 2019, this reference is no longer relevant) or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity, until the expiration of TWO MONTHS next after notice in writing has been delivered to, or left at the office of - (a) in the case of a suit against the Central Government, except where it relates to a railway, a Secretary to that Government; (b) in the case of a suit against the Central Government where it relates to a railway, the General Manager of that railway; (c) in the case of a suit against any other State Government, a Secretary to that Government or the Collector of the district; and, in the case of a public officer, delivered to him or left at his office, stating the cause of action, the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff and the relief which he claims; and the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left. (2) A suit to obtain an URGENT OR IMMEDIATE RELIEF against the Government or any public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity, may be instituted, with the leave of the court, without serving any notice as required by sub-section (1); but the court shall not grant relief in the suit, whether interim or otherwise, except after giving to the Government or public officer, as the case may be, a reasonable opportunity of showing cause in respect of the relief prayed for in the suit: provided that the court shall, if satisfied, after hearing the parties, that no urgent or immediate relief need be granted in the suit, return the plaint for presentation to it after complying with the requirements of sub-section (1). (3) No suit instituted against the Government or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity shall be dismissed merely by reason of any error or defect in the notice referred to in sub-section (1), if in such notice (a) the name, description and residence of the plaintiff had been so given as to enable the appropriate authority or the public officer to identify the person serving the notice and such notice had been delivered or left at the office of the appropriate authority specified in sub-section (1), and (b) the cause of action and the relief claimed by the plaintiff had been substantially indicated.

Object of Sec 80: to give the Government an opportunity to consider the claim and settle it without litigation, avoid unnecessary litigation and public funds. The section is MANDATORY and its terms are to be strictly complied with, subject to Sec 80(3) substantial compliance (Bihari Chowdhary v State of Bihar, 1984: the notice requirement is mandatory; Sec 80 is not an empty formality; State of Andhra Pradesh v Pioneer Builders, 2006). Sec 80 does not apply to (a) suits against Government for injunction or relief that is urgent (Sec 80(2)); (b) suits not 'against Government or public officer' such as suits by Government; (c) writ petitions; (d) ordinarily, suits against statutory corporations or government companies that are not 'the Government'; however, in 2025 the Supreme Court held that failure to serve the mandatory Sec 80 notice before suing a State-owned entity covered by the requirement rendered the resulting decree a nullity, open to challenge even at a later stage (verify the exact ruling). A notice under Sec 80 isn't needed where the suit is against a public officer for an act NOT done in his official capacity. Delay: two months must lapse; a suit filed before the expiry is premature; the defect may be cured by return of plaint and re-presentation. Limitation does not stop running during the notice period (Sec 15(2) Limitation Act - the period of notice is excluded if the notice is required by law: Sec 15(2) Limitation Act: in computing the period of limitation for any suit of which notice has been given, in accordance with the requirements of any enactment in force, the period of such notice shall be excluded).

Sec 81: exemption from arrest and personal appearance - a public officer shall not be arrested under Sec 55 or Order XXI and is exempt from personal appearance in respect of acts in official capacity, unless the court requires. Sec 82: EXECUTION OF DECREE AGAINST GOVERNMENT: (1) where, in a suit by or against the Government or against a public officer in respect of any such act as aforesaid, a decree is passed against the Union of India or a State or, as the case may be, the public officer, such decree shall not be executed unless it remains unsatisfied for the period of THREE MONTHS computed from the date of such decree; Verify the remaining sub-sections of Sec 82 in the bare Code.

ORDER XXVII - SUITS BY OR AGAINST THE GOVERNMENT OR PUBLIC OFFICERS IN THEIR OFFICIAL CAPACITY: Rule 1: persons authorised to act for the Government - the plaint shall be signed and verified by any person whom the Government may, by general or special order, appoint in this behalf, and shall be sufficient for any person so appointed to be acquainted with the facts; Rule 2: persons authorised to act for the Government in respect of suits; Rule 3: persons to be named as plaintiffs or defendants in suits by or against the Government; Rule 4: the Government pleader to be agent of the Government for the purpose of receiving processes (Rule 4: Government pleader is agent for service); Rule 5: appearance of Government - the court shall allow a reasonable time for the Government pleader to receive instructions; Rule 5A: where the suit is against a public officer for damages or other relief and the Government not joined, the Government shall be joined as a party (Rule 5A: where a suit is instituted against a public officer for damages in respect of an act alleged to be done by him in his official capacity, the Government shall be joined as a party to the suit); Rule 5B: duty of the court in suits against the Government or a public officer to assist in arriving at a settlement (Rule 5B: in every suit or proceeding to which the Government or a public officer acting in his official capacity is a party, the court shall make an endeavour at the first hearing of the suit, where it is possible according to the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit); Rule 8A: no security shall be required from the Government or from a public officer sued in an official capacity (no security for costs or costs of appeal required); Rule 8B: Government pleader; Order XXVII-A: notice to the Attorney-General or Advocate-General in suits involving substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or as to the validity of any statutory instrument (Rule 1: in any suit in which it appears to the court that any such question is involved, the court shall not proceed to determine that question until after notice has been given to the Attorney-General for India (where the question relates to the Constitution of India or validity of a statutory instrument) or the Advocate-General of the State). Government can be sued in tort subject to sovereign immunity doctrine (Kasturi Lal; Nilabati Behera).

sections.title: Institution of Suit, Plaint, Return and Rejection of Plaint (Sec 26, Orders IV and VII)
sections.summary: Order VII Rule 11 (rejection of plaint) is among the most litigated and most frequently examined provisions; with recent 2025-26 Supreme Court rulings it is a high-probability topic.
key_points: Sec 26: every suit shall be instituted by the presentation of a plaint or in such other manner as may be prescribed. In every plaint, facts shall be proved by affidavit (Sec 26(2), added 1999). Order IV Rule 1: every suit shall be instituted by presenting a plaint in duplicate to the court or such officer as it appoints; every plaint shall comply with the rules contained in Orders VI and VII; the plaint shall not be deemed duly instituted unless it complies with these requirements (Order IV Rule 1(3)). The date of institution = the date of presentation of a proper plaint (important for limitation). Order IV Rule 2: register of suits.

Order VII Rule 1 - PARTICULARS TO BE CONTAINED IN THE PLAINT: (a) the name of the court in which the suit is brought; (b) the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff; (c) the name, description and place of residence of the defendant, so far as they can be ascertained; (d) where the plaintiff or the defendant is a minor or a person of unsound mind, a statement to that effect; (e) the facts constituting the cause of action and when it arose; (f) the facts showing that the court has jurisdiction; (g) the relief which the plaintiff claims; (h) where the plaintiff has allowed a set-off or relinquished a portion of his claim, the amount so allowed or relinquished; and (i) a statement of the value of the subject-matter of the suit for the purposes of jurisdiction and of court-fees, so far as the case admits. Rule 2: suits for money - the precise amount claimed (except where the plaintiff sues for mesne profits, or for an amount which will be found due on taking unsettled accounts, or for movables of which valuation is not possible); Rule 3: suits for immovable property - the description must be sufficient to identify it (boundaries, survey number); Rule 4: where the plaintiff sues as a representative, the plaint must show that he has an actual existing interest in the subject-matter and has taken steps necessary to enable him to institute a suit concerning it; Rule 5: the defendant's interest and liability to be shown; Rule 6: GROUNDS OF EXEMPTION FROM LIMITATION LAW - where the suit is instituted after the expiration of the period prescribed by the law of limitation, the plaint shall show the ground upon which exemption from such law is claimed (Sec 14, 15 etc. of the Limitation Act); Rule 7: relief to be specifically stated (the court may grant any other relief to which the plaintiff is entitled - a prayer for 'such further or other relief' is sufficient for relief not specifically asked); Rule 8: relief founded on separate grounds to be stated separately; Rule 9: procedure on admitting plaint - the plaintiff must present as many copies as defendants, along with prescribed fee for service of summons (as amended 1999/ 2002 - copies on plain paper; delivery within 7 days); Rule 14: production of document on which plaintiff sues - where a plaintiff sues upon a document in his possession or power, he shall produce it in court when the plaint is presented, and shall at the same time deliver the document or a copy thereof to be filed with the plaint. A document not produced with the plaint cannot be received in evidence without leave of the court (Rule 14(3)); documents in plaintiff's possession but not relied upon in the suit (for cross-examination/ rebuttal) may be produced later (Rule 14(4)); Rule 15: where the document is not in the plaintiff's possession, he shall state in whose possession it is; Rule 17: production of shop-book.

VALUATION: for court fees (Court Fees Act 1870 and State laws) and for jurisdiction (Suits Valuation Act 1887); the plaintiff is the best judge of valuation (dominus litis) but the court may examine if manifestly undervalued (Order 7 Rule 11(b)). Nature of cause of action: 'cause of action' = bundle of facts necessary for the plaintiff to prove to get a decree - every fact which is material to be proved to entitle the plaintiff to succeed (Rule 11(a)). A plaint cannot be amended to introduce a fresh cause of action after limitation (subject to Order 6 Rule 17).

RETURN OF PLAINT - Order VII Rule 10: subject to the provisions of Rule 10A, the plaint shall at any stage of the suit be returned to be presented to the court in which the suit should have been instituted; (2) procedure on returning a plaint: the judge shall endorse on it the date of its presentation and return, the name of the party presenting it, and a brief statement of the reasons for returning it. Rule 10A: where the plaint is returned the court shall fix a date for the appearance of the parties in the court in which the plaint is proposed to be presented, and give notice (to avoid multiplicity - 2002 amendment). Return of plaint is for lack of territorial/ pecuniary jurisdiction (not for any other defect). The plaint, when re-presented, is treated as a fresh institution in the proper court, but Sec 14 of the Limitation Act (exclusion of time spent bona fide in a court without jurisdiction) applies; An order returning a plaint is appealable (Order 43 Rule 1(a)) except where the procedure under Rule 10A has been followed.

REJECTION OF PLAINT - Order VII Rule 11: the plaint shall be rejected in the following cases: (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action; (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so; (c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is returned upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so; (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law; (e) where it is not filed in duplicate; (f) where the plaintiff fails to comply with the provisions of Rule 9. PROVISO: the time fixed by the court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not be extended unless the court, for reasons to be recorded, is satisfied that the plaintiff was prevented by any cause of an exceptional nature from correcting the valuation or supplying the requisite stamp-paper, as the case may be, within the time fixed by the court and that refusal to extend such time would cause grave injustice to the plaintiff. Rule 12: where a plaint is rejected the judge shall record an order to that effect with the reasons for such order. Rule 13: the rejection of the plaint on any of the grounds hereinbefore mentioned shall not of its own force preclude the plaintiff from presenting a fresh plaint in respect of the same cause of action.

PRINCIPLES (Supreme Court): (1) the power under Rule 11 is drastic; the court looks ONLY at the averments in the PLAINT (and documents filed with it) and assumes them to be true; the defence, written statement or the defendant's documents cannot be looked at (Saleem Bhai v State of Maharashtra, 2003; Liverpool & London S.P. & I Association v M.V. Sea Success I, 2004; Dahiben v Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali, 2020 - the plaint must be read as a whole; clever drafting creating an illusion of cause of action must be detected and nipped in the bud: T. Arivandandam v T.V. Satyapal, 1977); (2) the question of 'bar of limitation' can be a ground under Rule 11(d) only if the plaint on its face shows the suit to be time-barred - mixed questions of law and fact require trial (the Supreme Court in N. Asha Devi v R. Aravind Kumar, 2026 INSC 908, reiterated that a plaint can be rejected where the limitation bar is apparent on the face of the plaint - verify); (3) RES JUDICATA ordinarily cannot be a ground for rejection under Rule 11(d) as it involves mixed questions of fact and law (SC, July 2025); (4) the court-fee/ valuation question: Rule 11(b)-(c) requires the court to call upon the plaintiff to correct valuation; where the question of valuation requires evidence, a plaint cannot be rejected at the threshold and the issue can be decided after evidence (Neelam Sharma v Amita Passan, 2026 INSC 913 - verify); (5) PARTIAL REJECTION is not permissible - the plaint must be rejected as a whole, not in part (Sejal Glass Ltd v Navilan Merchants, 2018; Madhav Prasad Aggarwal v Axis Bank, 2019); (6) an application under Rule 11 can be made at any stage of the suit - even before issues, even after the written statement - but a second application on the same ground is barred by interlocutory res judicata (B.S. Lalitha v Bhuvanesh, 2026 INSC 499); (7) a plaint rejected under Rule 11 results in a DECREE (Sec 2(2)), appealable under Sec 96; an order REFUSING to reject is not a decree and is not appealable (it may be challenged by a revision or under Art 227 - and as the Supreme Court noted in a 2026 matter 'no appeal lies against the rejection of an application under Order VII Rule 11'); (8) 'barred by any law' - includes bar by limitation, by a statute (e.g., Sec 80 non-compliance is not a bar as such but a defect), by Sec 34 SARFAESI, Sec 9 CPC ouster, Benami Act, etc.; the bar must appear from the plaint; (9) vexatious litigation; 'meritless' suits - illusory cause of action; (10) Order VII Rule 11 and Sec 151: the court has inherent power to reject plaint in the interest of justice only within Rule 11's grounds.

AMENDMENT AND VERIFICATION: Order 6 Rule 17 (see 2.4) allows amendment of plaint; the plaint can be amended even after limitation if the amendment is merely formal or does not change the nature of the suit or cause of action. Plaint verification (Order 6 Rule 15) and an affidavit (Sec 26(2)) are mandatory; non-verification is a curable defect. Signature and pleadings: Order 6 Rule 14. Return and Rejection: difference - return is for want of territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction; rejection is for substantive defects; return does not terminate the suit; rejection does and also results in a decree (deemed), though a fresh plaint is allowed (Rule 13).

sections.title: Parties to Suits and Joinder (Order I, Order II) and Representative Suits
sections.summary: Joinder of parties, necessary vs proper parties, misjoinder/ non-joinder, representative suits (Order I Rule 8) and the rule against splitting claims (Order II Rule 2).
key_points: ORDER I RULE 1 - JOINDER OF PLAINTIFFS: all persons may be joined in one suit as plaintiffs in whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally or in the alternative, where, if such persons brought separate suits, any common question of law or fact would arise. Rule 3 - JOINDER OF DEFENDANTS: all persons may be joined as defendants against whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally, or in the alternative, where, if separate suits were brought against such persons, any common question of law or fact would arise. Rule 3A: separate trials - if it appears that joinder may embarrass or delay trial, the court may order separate trials. Rule 4: judgment may be given for or against one or more of joint parties. Rule 5: defendant need not be interested in all the relief claimed. Rule 6: joint contractors - plaintiff may join. Rule 7: when plaintiff in doubt from whom redress is to be obtained (alternative defendants).

Rule 9 - MISJOINDER AND NON-JOINDER: no suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties, and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it. Proviso: nothing in this rule shall apply to non-joinder of a NECESSARY PARTY. Rule 10 - SUIT IN NAME OF WRONG PLAINTIFF; ADDITION AND STRIKING OUT OF PARTIES: (1) where a suit has been instituted in the name of the wrong person as plaintiff, or where it is doubtful whether it has been instituted in the name of the right plaintiff, the court may at any stage of the suit, if satisfied that the suit has been instituted through a bona fide mistake, and that it is necessary for the determination of the real matter in dispute so to do, order any other person to be substituted or added as plaintiff upon such terms as the court thinks just. (2) the court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added. (3) no person shall be added as a plaintiff suing without a next friend or as the next friend of a plaintiff under any disability without his consent. (4) where a defendant is added the plaint shall, unless the court otherwise directs, be amended in such manner as may be necessary, and amended copies of the summons and of the plaint shall be served on the new defendant and, if the court thinks fit, on the original defendants. (5) subject to the provisions of the Limitation Act 1963, Sec 21, the proceedings as against any person added as defendant shall be deemed to have begun only on the service of the summons. Rule 13: all objections on the ground of non-joinder or misjoinder of parties shall be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and, in all cases where issues are settled, at or before such settlement, unless the ground of objection has subsequently arisen, and any such objection not so taken shall be deemed to have been waived.

NECESSARY PARTY vs PROPER PARTY: Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v Additional Member, Board of Revenue (1963): a NECESSARY party is one without whom no order can be made effectively; a PROPER party is one in whose absence an effective order can be made but whose presence is necessary for a complete and final decision on the question involved. TWO TESTS for a necessary party: (1) there must be a right to some relief against such party in respect of the matter involved in the proceeding in question; (2) it should not be possible to pass an effective decree in the absence of such a party. Kasturi v Iyyamperumal (2005): in a suit for specific performance of an agreement for sale, a person who claims title adverse to the vendor is not a necessary party as the only issue is whether the agreement is enforceable against the vendor; Mumbai International Airport (P) Ltd v Regency Convention Centre & Hotels (2010): the plaintiff is the dominus litis and cannot be compelled to sue a person against whom he claims no relief - the court may add a party only if he is a necessary or proper party; a person who has no direct interest in the subject-matter cannot be added merely because he may be affected indirectly; Sumtibai v Paras Finance Co (2007); Ramesh Hirachand Kundanmal v Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay (1992): the court has wide discretion to add a person whose presence is necessary to adjudicate effectively. Transposition of parties: the court may transpose a defendant to plaintiff (Order 23 Rule 1A).

ORDER I RULE 8 - REPRESENTATIVE SUITS: (1) where there are numerous persons having the same interest in one suit, one or more of such persons may, with the permission of the court, sue or be sued, or may defend such suit, on behalf of, or for the benefit of, all persons so interested; but the court shall in such case give, at the plaintiff's expense, notice of the institution of the suit to all such persons either by personal service or, where from the number of persons or any other cause such service is not reasonably practicable, by public advertisement, as the court in each case may direct. (2) the court may direct that one or more of the persons may sue or be sued... (4) any person on whose behalf or for whose benefit a suit is instituted, or defended, under sub-rule (1), may apply to the court to be made a party to such suit. (5) where any person suing or defending in any such suit does not proceed with due diligence in the suit or defence, the court may substitute in his place any other person having the same interest in the suit. (6) a decree passed in a suit under this rule shall be binding on all persons on whose behalf, or for whose benefit, the suit is instituted, or defended, as the case may be (Explanation: the persons not having the same interest as the representative are not bound). Rule 8(6) and Sec 11 Explanation VI. Rule 8 requires 'same interest' (Kumaravelu Chettiar v T.P. Ramaswamy Ayyar, 1933 - test: same interest need not be identical but a common interest); Rule 8 applies to suits concerning rights of many persons, such as members of a community, public rights, or a sect; in a representative suit, withdrawal/ compromise needs the court's permission and notice (Order 23 Rule 3B). Class action: Order I Rule 8 and Sec 91-92 for public interest; Companies Act Sec 245 for class actions in company law.

ORDER II - FRAMING OF SUIT: Rule 1: every suit shall as far as practicable be so framed as to afford ground for final decision upon the subjects in dispute and to prevent further litigation concerning them. RULE 2 - SUIT TO INCLUDE THE WHOLE CLAIM: (1) every suit shall include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action; but a plaintiff may relinquish any portion of his claim in order to bring the suit within the jurisdiction of any court. (2) where a plaintiff omits to sue in respect of, or intentionally relinquishes, any portion of his claim, he shall not afterwards sue in respect of the portion so omitted or relinquished. (3) a person entitled to more than one relief in respect of the same cause of action may sue for all or any of such reliefs; but if he omits, except with the leave of the court, to sue for all such reliefs, he shall not afterwards sue for any relief so omitted. Explanation: an obligation and a collateral security for its performance and successive claims arising under the same obligation shall be deemed respectively to constitute but one cause of action. PRINCIPLES: the bar applies where the later suit is based on the SAME CAUSE OF ACTION as the earlier suit (Gurbux Singh v Bhooralal, 1964: the defendant must plead and prove the bar by producing the earlier plaint; the question whether the cause of action is the same is determined by comparing the pleadings; the bar does not apply where the plaintiff could not have claimed the omitted relief (e.g., relief not available at the time of the first suit)); Sec 11 and Order 2 Rule 2: res judicata is based on decision; Order 2 Rule 2 on omission to claim; Order 2 Rule 2 does not apply to execution proceedings, nor to a case where the first suit is withdrawn with permission (Order 23 Rule 1), nor to suit for possession after a suit for declaration where leave is obtained. Rule 3: joinder of causes of action - the plaintiff may unite in the same suit several causes of action against the same defendant or the same defendants jointly; Rule 4: only certain claims to be joined for recovery of immovable property (mesne profits or arrears of rent, damages for breach of contract under which the property is held, claims for which the plaintiff is entitled to relief arising out of the same transaction); Rule 6: court may order separate trials; Rule 7: objections for misjoinder of causes of action to be taken at the earliest opportunity.

Related: ORDER III - recognised agents and pleaders: Rule 1: any appearance, application or act in or to any court, required or authorised by law to be made or done by a party in such court, may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force, be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognised agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf; Rule 2: recognised agents - persons holding powers-of-attorney authorising them to make such appearances and applications and do such acts on behalf of parties, and persons carrying on trade or business for and in the names of parties not resident within the local limits of the court; Rule 4: appointment of a pleader (vakalatnama); no pleader shall act for any person in any court unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person; Rule 4(2): the appointment shall be filed in court and shall remain in force until determined with the leave of the court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader; Rule 6: service of process on recognised agent. Order III Rule 1-2 and the power of attorney holder: a power of attorney holder can depose only about what he has personal knowledge of (Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v Indusind Bank, 2005); he cannot depose for the principal on matters in the personal knowledge of the principal.
