sections.title: Death, Marriage and Insolvency of Parties; Withdrawal and Compromise (Orders XXII and XXIII)
sections.summary: Abatement, substitution of legal representatives, limitation for substitution (90 days) and setting aside abatement (60 days), withdrawal with liberty (Order 23 Rule 1) and compromise decrees (Rule 3) are routine questions.
key_points: ORDER XXII Rule 1: the death of a plaintiff or defendant shall not cause the suit to abate if the right to sue survives. Rule 2: where there are more than one plaintiff or defendant, and any of them dies, and where the right to sue survives against or to the surviving defendant or defendants alone, or to the surviving plaintiff or plaintiffs alone, the court shall cause an entry to that effect to be made on the record and the suit shall proceed at the instance of the surviving plaintiff(s) or against the surviving defendant(s). Rule 3 - PROCEDURE IN CASE OF DEATH OF ONE OF SEVERAL PLAINTIFFS OR OF SOLE PLAINTIFF: (1) where one of two or more plaintiffs dies and the right to sue does not survive to the surviving plaintiff or plaintiffs alone, or a sole plaintiff or sole surviving plaintiff dies and the right to sue survives, the court, on an application made in that behalf, shall cause the legal representative of the deceased plaintiff to be made a party and shall proceed with the suit. (2) where within the time limited by law no application is made under sub-rule (1), the suit shall ABATE so far as the deceased plaintiff is concerned, and, on the application of the defendant, the court may award to him the costs which he may have incurred in defending the suit, to be recovered from the estate of the deceased plaintiff. Rule 4 - PROCEDURE IN CASE OF DEATH OF ONE OF SEVERAL DEFENDANTS OR OF SOLE DEFENDANT: (1) where one of two or more defendants dies and the right to sue does not survive against the surviving defendant or defendants alone, or a sole defendant or sole surviving defendant dies and the right to sue survives, the court, on an application made in that behalf, shall cause the legal representative of the deceased defendant to be made a party and shall proceed with the suit. (2) any person so made a party may make any defence appropriate to his character as legal representative of the deceased defendant. (3) where within the time limited by law no application is made under sub-rule (1), the suit shall abate as against the deceased defendant. (4) the court whenever it thinks fit, may exempt the plaintiff from the necessity of substituting the legal representatives of any such defendant who has failed to file a written statement or who, having filed it, has failed to appear and contest the suit at the hearing; and judgment may, in such case, be pronounced against the said defendant notwithstanding the death of such defendant and shall have the same force and effect as if it has been pronounced before death took place. (5) where the question arises as to whether any person is or is not the legal representative of a deceased plaintiff or deceased defendant, such question shall be determined by the court (Rule 5).

Rule 6 - NO ABATEMENT BY REASON OF DEATH AFTER HEARING: notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing rules, whether the cause of action survives or not, there shall be no abatement by reason of the death of either party between the conclusion of the hearing and the pronouncing of the judgment, but judgment may in such case be pronounced notwithstanding the death and shall have the same force and effect as if it had been pronounced before the death took place. Rule 7: marriage of a female party (no abatement; suit continues); Rule 8: insolvency of plaintiff - the suit shall not abate by reason only of the insolvency of the plaintiff, but the assignee or receiver may continue the suit or give security for costs; if he fails, the suit may be dismissed on the application of the defendant. RULE 9 - EFFECT OF ABATEMENT OR DISMISSAL: (1) where a suit abates or is dismissed under this Order, no fresh suit shall be brought on the same cause of action. (2) the plaintiff or the person claiming to be the legal representative of a deceased plaintiff or the assignee or the receiver in insolvency, where the suit has abated or has been dismissed under this Order, may apply for an order to set aside the abatement or dismissal; and if it is proved that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from continuing the suit, the court shall set aside the abatement or dismissal upon such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit. (3) the provisions of Sec 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 shall apply to applications under sub-rule (2). Rule 10 - procedure in case of assignment before final order in suit: the suit may be continued by or against the person to or upon whom the interest has devolved with the leave of the court (an assignee/ transferee pendente lite); Rule 10A: duty of pleader to communicate to the court the death of a party; Rule 11: application of Order to appeals (the word 'plaintiff' includes appellant, 'defendant' includes respondent); Rule 12: Order not to apply to proceedings in execution of a decree or order (Rules 3, 4, 8 do not apply to execution proceedings).

LIMITATION (Limitation Act 1963): application to implead legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff/ appellant/ defendant/ respondent - NINETY days from the date of death (Art 120); application to set aside abatement - SIXTY days from the date of abatement (Art 121) - abatement takes place on the expiry of the 90 days, automatically, without any order of the court; application for condonation of delay under Sec 5 along with Rule 9(2). Principles: (1) abatement is automatic and the suit stands abated once the period lapses; no order is needed; (2) where one of the several plaintiffs/ appellants dies and the right to sue survives to the others, there is no abatement unless the interest is joint and indivisible; (3) in JOINT AND INDIVISIBLE decree appeals, if the legal representatives of one deceased respondent are not brought on record, the entire appeal abates (State of Punjab v Nathu Ram, 1962; Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v Pramod Gupta, 2003: where the decree is joint and inseverable, abatement of the appeal against one respondent leads to abatement of the whole appeal; the test being whether the decree could be inconsistent or contradictory if the appeal proceeds); (4) substitution of legal heirs can be sought even after notice; the court should be liberal in setting aside abatement as the delay is for sufficient cause (Mithailal Dalsangar Singh v Annabai Devram Kini, 2003: the court should take a liberal view in setting aside abatement, since procedural technicalities should not defeat substantive rights); (5) Order 22 Rule 4 requires the legal representatives of a deceased defendant to be substituted; where the court exempts the plaintiff (Rule 4(4)); (6) The Supreme Court in a 2025 ruling explained the correct procedure for an application to substitute legal heirs, set aside the abatement and condone delay under Order XXII Rules 3, 4 and 9 (the court should ordinarily treat the application as a composite application) - verify. A decree passed against a dead person without substitution is a nullity unless Rule 4(4)/ Rule 6 applies (Order 22 Rule 4(4) cures when the defendant failed to file a written statement).

ORDER XXIII - WITHDRAWAL AND ADJUSTMENT OF SUITS: Rule 1 - WITHDRAWAL OF SUIT OR ABANDONMENT OF PART OF CLAIM: (1) at any time after the institution of a suit, the plaintiff may as against all or any of the defendants abandon his suit or abandon a part of his claim; provided that where the plaintiff is a minor or other person to whom the provisions of Rules 1 to 14 of Order XXXII extend, neither the suit nor any part of the claim shall be abandoned without the leave of the court. (2) an application for leave under the proviso to sub-rule (1) shall be accompanied by an affidavit of the next friend and also, if the minor or such other person is represented by a pleader, by a certificate of the pleader to the effect that the abandonment proposed is, in his opinion, for the benefit of the minor or such other person. (3) where the court is satisfied (a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or (b) that there are sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim, it may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or such part of the claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of the claim. (4) where the plaintiff (a) abandons any suit or part of claim under sub-rule (1), or (b) withdraws from a suit or part of a claim without the permission referred to in sub-rule (3), he shall be liable for such costs as the court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim. (5) nothing in this rule shall be deemed to authorise the court to permit one of several plaintiffs to abandon a suit or part of a claim under sub-rule (1), or to withdraw, under sub-rule (3), any suit or part of a claim, without the consent of the other plaintiff. Rule 1A: when transposition of defendants as plaintiffs may be permitted. Rule 2: limitation law not affected by first suit - in any fresh suit instituted on permission granted under Rule 1, the plaintiff shall be bound by the law of limitation in the same manner as if the first suit had not been instituted. Formal defect = a defect of the nature which is not related to merits (Sec 14 Limitation Act might apply).

RULE 3 - COMPROMISE OF SUIT: where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise in writing and signed by the parties, or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit, the court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the parties to the suit, whether or not the subject-matter of the agreement, compromise or satisfaction is the same as the subject-matter of the suit; provided that where it is alleged by one party and denied by the other that an adjustment or satisfaction has been arrived at, the court shall decide the question; but no adjournment shall be granted for the purpose of deciding the question, unless the court, for reasons to be recorded, thinks fit to grant such adjournment. Explanation: an agreement or compromise which is void or voidable under the Indian Contract Act 1872 shall not be deemed to be lawful within the meaning of this rule. RULE 3A - BAR TO SUIT: no suit shall lie to set aside a decree on the ground that the compromise on which the decree is based was not lawful. Rule 3B: no agreement or compromise in a representative suit (Sec 92 suits, Order 1 Rule 8 suits) shall be entered into without the leave of the court expressly recorded in the proceedings; and the court shall give notice to persons interested. Rule 4: proceedings in execution of decree or order not affected. Consent decree: Pushpa Devi Bhagat v Rajinder Singh (2006): (1) no appeal lies against a consent decree (Sec 96(3)); (2) the only remedy of a party who claims that the consent decree was not lawful is to approach the same court which recorded the compromise (under the proviso to Rule 3 - to contend that no compromise was arrived at); (3) no separate suit (Rule 3A); (4) Order 43 Rule 1(m) appeal lies against an order refusing to record a compromise. A consent decree operates as an estoppel; its terms are contractual; the court must be satisfied that the compromise is lawful and the parties have authority (a pleader's compromise requires express authority - Byram Pestonji Gariwala v Union Bank of India, 1992; Banwari Lal v Chando Devi, 1993: compromise in a suit by minors/ representatives - court's duty to examine). A compromise decree isn't a decision on merits so it doesn't constitute res judicata strictly but binds by estoppel.

Withdrawal WITH permission and liberty (Rule 1(3)) - fresh suit allowed; withdrawal WITHOUT permission - fresh suit barred (Rule 1(4)).
Rule 3A: no suit to set aside a compromise decree; no appeal (Sec 96(3)).

No abatement if death occurs after the conclusion of the hearing (Rule 6).

sections.title: Special Parties: Corporations, Firms, Minors and Persons of Unsound Mind, Indigent Persons (Orders XXIX, XXX, XXXII, XXXIII)
sections.summary: Next friend/ guardian ad litem, compromise by guardian (Order 32 Rule 7), suits against firms in firm name (Order 30), indigent person rules (Order 33 Rule 5).
key_points: ORDER XXIX - SUITS BY OR AGAINST CORPORATIONS: Rule 1: in suits by or against a corporation, any pleading may be signed and verified on behalf of the corporation by the secretary or by any director or other principal officer of the corporation who is able to depose to the facts of the case. Rule 2: service on corporation: subject to any statutory provision regulating service of process, where the suit is against a corporation, the summons may be served (a) on the secretary, or on any director, or other principal officer of the corporation, or (b) by leaving it or sending it by post addressed to the corporation at the registered office, or if there is no registered office then at the place where the corporation carries on business. Rule 3: power to require personal appearance of officer of the corporation.

ORDER XXX - SUITS BY OR AGAINST FIRMS AND PERSONS CARRYING ON BUSINESS IN NAMES OTHER THAN THEIR OWN: Rule 1: any two or more persons claiming or being liable as partners and carrying on business in India may sue or be sued in the name of the firm (if any) of which such persons were partners at the time of the accruing of the cause of action, and any party to a suit may in such case apply to the court for a statement of the names and addresses of the persons who were, at the time of the accruing of the cause of action, partners in such firm, to be furnished and verified in such manner as the court may direct. Rule 2: disclosure of partners' names - where persons sue or are sued as partners in the name of their firm, the plaintiffs or their pleader shall on demand in writing by or on behalf of any defendant, forthwith declare in writing the names and places of residence of all the persons constituting the firm. Rule 3: service - where persons are sued as partners in the name of their firm, the summons shall be served either (a) upon any one or more of the partners, or (b) at the principal place at which the partnership business is carried on within India upon any person having, at the time of service, the control or management of the partnership business there, as the court may direct, and such service shall be deemed good service upon the firm so sued, whether all or any of the partners are within or without India. Rule 4: right of suit on death of partner (it is not necessary to join the legal representatives of the deceased partner). Rule 5: notice in what capacity served - where a summons is issued to a firm and is served in the manner provided by Rule 3, every person upon whom it is served shall be informed by notice in writing given at the time of such service whether he is served as a partner or as a person having the control or management of the partnership business, or in both characters, and, in default of such notice, the person served shall be deemed to be served as a partner. Rule 6: appearance of partners individually; Rule 7: no appearance except by partners (a person served as a person in control of business cannot appear except as a partner); Rule 8: appearance under protest - any person served as a partner may appear under protest denying that he is a partner; Rule 9: suits between co-partners (the Order applies to suits between a firm and one or more of its partners and between firms having one or more common partners); Rule 10: suits against persons carrying on business in name other than their own - the person may be sued in such name. A firm is not a legal entity; a decree against a firm can be executed against the firm's property or the partners' personal property if they were served or appeared as partners (Order 21 Rule 50). Registration under the Partnership Act Sec 69 bars suits by unregistered firms for contractual rights (not applicable to suits against the firm).

ORDER XXXII - SUITS BY OR AGAINST MINORS AND PERSONS OF UNSOUND MIND: Rule 1: every suit by a minor shall be instituted in his name by a person who in such suit shall be called the NEXT FRIEND of the minor. Rule 2: where a suit is instituted by or on behalf of a minor without a next friend, the defendant may apply to have the plaint taken off the file, with costs to be paid by the pleader or other person by whom it was presented; Rule 3: GUARDIAN FOR THE SUIT - where the defendant is a minor, the court, on being satisfied of the fact of his minority, shall appoint a proper person to be guardian for the suit for such minor (the court may appoint the court officer or a person who has no adverse interest); service on the guardian ad litem; a decree passed against a minor without a guardian being appointed is voidable (not a nullity) unless prejudice - Walian v Banke Behari (1903). Rule 3A: no decree shall be set aside merely on the ground that the next friend or guardian for the suit of a minor had an interest in the subject-matter of the suit adverse to that of the minor, but the fact that such next friend or guardian had such an adverse interest shall be a ground for revising the decree if the interests of the minor were prejudiced (revision/ review/ appeal). Rule 4: WHO MAY ACT AS NEXT FRIEND OR BE APPOINTED GUARDIAN FOR THE SUIT: (1) any person who is of sound mind and has attained majority may act as next friend of a minor or as his guardian for the suit, provided that the interest of such person is not adverse to that of the minor and that he is not, in the case of a next friend, a defendant, or, in the case of a guardian for the suit, a plaintiff. (2) where a minor has a guardian appointed or declared by competent authority, no person other than such guardian shall act as the next friend of the minor or be appointed his guardian for the suit unless the court considers, for reasons to be recorded, that it is for the minor's welfare that another person be permitted to act or be appointed. Rule 5: representation of minor by next friend or guardian for the suit - every application to the court on behalf of a minor other than an application under Rule 10(2) shall be made by his next friend or by his guardian for the suit; Rule 6: receipt by next friend or guardian for the suit of property under a decree for the minor - without the leave of the court; Rule 7 - AGREEMENT OR COMPROMISE BY NEXT FRIEND OR GUARDIAN FOR THE SUIT: (1) no next friend or guardian for the suit shall, without the leave of the court expressly recorded in the proceedings, enter into any agreement or compromise on behalf of a minor with reference to the suit in which he acts as next friend or guardian. (2) any such agreement or compromise entered into without the leave of the court so recorded shall be VOIDABLE against all parties other than the minor. Rule 11: removal of guardian for the suit; Rule 12: retirement/ removal/ death of next friend; Rule 15: Rules 1 to 14 apply to persons of unsound mind (and to persons who by reason of mental infirmity are incapable of protecting their interests). A minor is bound by a decree properly passed after due representation; The court must be satisfied that a compromise is for the benefit of the minor.

ORDER XXXIII - SUITS BY INDIGENT PERSONS: Rule 1: subject to the following provisions, any suit may be instituted by an indigent person. Explanation I: a person is an 'indigent person' if he is not possessed of sufficient means (other than property exempt from attachment in execution of a decree and the subject-matter of the suit) to enable him to pay the fee prescribed by law for the plaint in such suit, or, where no such fee is prescribed, if he is not entitled to property worth one thousand rupees other than the property exempt from attachment in execution of a decree, and the subject-matter of the suit. Explanation II: any property which is acquired by a person after the presentation of his application for permission to sue as an indigent person, and before the decision of the application, shall be taken into account in considering the question whether or not the applicant is an indigent person. Rule 2: contents of application; Rule 3: presentation of application by the applicant in person (unless exempted); Rule 4: examination of applicant; Rule 5 - REJECTION OF APPLICATION: the court shall reject an application for permission to sue as an indigent person (a) where it is not framed and presented in the manner prescribed by Rules 2 and 3; (b) where the applicant is not an indigent person; (c) where he has, within two months next before the presentation of the application, disposed of any property fraudulently or in order to be able to apply for permission to sue as an indigent person; provided that no application shall be rejected if, even after the value of the property disposed of by the applicant is taken into account, the applicant would be entitled to sue as an indigent person; (d) where his allegations do not show a cause of action; (e) where he has entered into any agreement with reference to the subject-matter of the proposed suit under which any other person has obtained an interest in such subject-matter; (f) where the allegations made by the applicant in the application show that the suit would be barred by any law for the time being in force; (g) where any other person has entered into an agreement with him to finance the litigation. Rule 7: procedure at the hearing - the court shall examine the witnesses and decide; Rule 8: procedure if application admitted - it shall be numbered and registered and shall be deemed the plaint in the suit, and the suit shall proceed in all other respects as a suit instituted in the ordinary manner, except that the plaintiff shall not be liable to pay any court-fee (other than fees payable for service of process) in respect of any petition, appointment of a pleader or other proceeding connected with the suit; Rule 9: removal from indigency (court may order the plaintiff to pay the fee if he becomes possessed of means - Rule 9: the court may withdraw the permission to sue as an indigent person where (a) he is guilty of vexatious or improper conduct; (b) it appears that his means are such that he ought not to continue to sue as an indigent person; or (c) he has entered into an agreement with another person under which such person has obtained an interest in the subject-matter); Rule 10: costs; Rule 11: procedure where indigent person succeeds - the court shall calculate the amount of court-fees which would have been paid by the plaintiff if he had not been permitted to sue as an indigent person; such amount shall be a first charge on the subject-matter of the suit; Rule 12: where the plaintiff fails - the court shall order him to pay the court fees; Rule 15: REFUSAL TO ALLOW APPLICANT TO SUE AS INDIGENT PERSON BARS SUBSEQUENT APPLICATION OF LIKE NATURE - an order refusing to allow the applicant to sue as an indigent person shall be a bar to any subsequent application of the like nature by him in respect of the same right to sue, but the applicant shall be at liberty to institute a suit in the ordinary manner in respect of such right, provided that he first pays the costs (if any) incurred by the State Government and by the opposite party in opposing his application for leave to sue as an indigent person. Rule 18: Government may provide pleader to an unrepresented indigent person (legal aid); Order 44: appeals by indigent persons (Order 44 Rule 1: any person entitled to prefer an appeal who is unable to pay the fee required for the memorandum of appeal may present an application accompanied by a memorandum of appeal, and may be allowed to appeal as an indigent person subject to the provisions relating to suits by indigent persons).
common_traps: Order 32 Rule 7: compromise on behalf of a minor without the leave of the court is VOIDABLE against all parties other than the minor.
Order 32 Rule 3A: adverse interest of next friend/ guardian - a ground for revising the decree.
Order 33 Rule 5: application is rejected where the applicant is not indigent, no cause of action, financing by another, etc.
Order 30: a firm is sued in the firm's name; service on any partner or person in control suffices; Rule 8: appearance under protest.
Order 33 Rule 15: refusal bars a subsequent application, but not an ordinary suit upon payment of costs.
likely_questions: Suit by a minor: through a next friend (Order 32 Rule 1).
Compromise on behalf of a minor needs: leave of the court (Rule 7).
Indigent person: Order 33; rejection grounds: Rule 5.
Suits by or against firms: Order 30.

sections.title: Public Nuisance and Public Charities (Secs 91-93), Interpleader (Sec 88, Order XXXV), Mortgage Suits (Order XXXIV) and Other Special Orders
sections.summary: Sections 91-92 (who may sue and with what leave) and the structure of Order 34 mortgage decrees are the main targets.
key_points: Sec 91 - PUBLIC NUISANCES AND OTHER WRONGFUL ACTS AFFECTING THE PUBLIC: (1) in the case of a public nuisance or other wrongful act affecting, or likely to affect, the public, a suit for a declaration and injunction or for such other relief as may be appropriate in the circumstances of the case may be instituted, (a) by the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons by reason of such public nuisance or other wrongful act. (2) nothing in sub-section (1) shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any right of suit which may exist independently of its provisions. Hence a private person who suffers SPECIAL DAMAGE (damage over and above that suffered by the public) can sue independently without leave (common law right preserved by Sec 91(2) - Rule that a private individual may sue for public nuisance only if he proves special damage). Sec 91 applies to public nuisance, such as obstruction of a highway, pollution; the relief is declaration and injunction (not damages).

Sec 92 - PUBLIC CHARITIES: (1) in the case of any alleged breach of any express or constructive trust created for public purposes of a charitable or religious nature, or where the direction of the court is deemed necessary for the administration of any such trust, the Advocate-General, or two or more persons having an interest in the trust and having obtained the leave of the court, may institute a suit, whether contentious or not, in the principal civil court of original jurisdiction or in any other court empowered in that behalf by the State Government within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the trust is situate, to obtain a decree - (a) removing any trustee; (b) appointing a new trustee; (c) vesting any property in a trustee; (cc) directing a trustee who has been removed or a person who has ceased to be a trustee, to deliver possession of any trust property in his possession to the person entitled to the possession of such property; (d) directing accounts and inquiries; (e) declaring what proportion of the trust property or of the interest therein shall be allocated to any particular object of the trust; (f) authorising the whole or any part of the trust property to be let, sold, mortgaged or exchanged; (g) settling a scheme; or (h) granting such further or other relief as the nature of the case may require. (2) subject to the provisions of the Religious Endowments Act 1863, no suit claiming any of the reliefs specified in sub-section (1) shall be instituted in respect of any such trust as is therein referred to except in conformity with the provisions of that sub-section. Essentials for Sec 92: (i) the trust is public (not private) and for charitable or religious purposes; (ii) there is an alleged breach of trust or direction of the court is necessary for administration; (iii) the suit is for one of the reliefs in sub-section (1); (iv) the suit is by the Advocate-General or two or more persons having an interest with leave of court. Where the suit is to vindicate the personal/ individual right of the plaintiff, Sec 92 doesn't apply (it must be representative - Vidyodaya Trust v Mohan Prasad R., 2008; Swami Paramatmanand Saraswati v Ramji Tripathi, 1974: the true nature of the suit; Charan Singh v Darshan Singh, 1975). The leave is a safeguard against frivolous suits; permission must be applied for and the court must be satisfied prima facie about the breach; the plaintiffs must have an interest in the trust. Sec 93: exercise of powers of the Advocate-General outside presidency towns - by the Collector or by any officer specially appointed. Public interest litigation in the High Court and Supreme Court (Art 226/32) supplements Secs 91-92.

INTERPLEADER SUITS - Sec 88: where two or more persons claim adversely to one another the same debt, sum of money or other property, movable or immovable, from another person, who claims no interest therein other than for charges or costs and who is ready to pay or deliver it to the rightful claimant, such other person may institute a suit of interpleader against all the claimants for the purpose of obtaining a decision as to the person to whom the payment or delivery shall be made and of obtaining indemnity for himself: provided that where any suit is pending in which the rights of all the parties can properly be decided, no such suit of interpleader shall be instituted. ORDER XXXV - Rule 1: plaint in an interpleader-suit - in every plaint in an interpleader suit, in addition to the other statements necessary for plaints, it must be stated (a) that the plaintiff claims no interest in the subject-matter in dispute other than for charges or costs; (b) the claims made by the defendants severally; and (c) that there is no collusion between the plaintiff and any of the defendants. Rule 2: payment of thing claimed into court; Rule 3: where the thing claimed is capable of being paid into court or placed in the custody of the court, the plaintiff may be required to so deposit before obtaining any order in the suit; Rule 4: procedure where defendant is suing plaintiff - the court may stay the suit and decide in the interpleader; Rule 5: procedure at the first hearing - the court may declare that the plaintiff is discharged from all liability to the claimants in respect of the thing claimed, award him his costs, and dismiss him from the suit; Rule 6: charges of plaintiff. Interpleader essentials: (1) two or more persons claiming adversely the same debt or property; (2) from a stakeholder who claims no interest (other than charges or costs); (3) stakeholder is ready to deliver to the rightful claimant; (4) no collusion; (5) no pending suit in which the rights of all can be decided. Order 36: SPECIAL CASE - parties to any suit may agree to state the questions of law or fact for the opinion of the court in the form of a special case (Rule 1), and the court shall hear and determine (Rule 3) and judgment shall be pronounced as in other suits; Order 24: payment into court - Rule 1: the defendant in any suit to recover a debt or damages may, at any stage of the suit, deposit in court such sum of money as he considers a satisfaction in full of the claim; Rule 2: notice of deposit to the plaintiff; Rule 3: interest on deposit not allowed to plaintiff after the notice; Rule 4: procedure where the plaintiff accepts as satisfaction in full or part. Order 25: security for costs - Rule 1: at any stage of a suit the court may, either of its own motion or on the application of any defendant, order the plaintiff to give security for the payment of all costs incurred and likely to be incurred by any defendant where it appears to the court that the sole plaintiff is, or (when there are more than one) that all the plaintiffs are, residing out of India, and that such plaintiff does not possess any sufficient immovable property within India other than the property in suit,; failure to furnish security results in dismissal of the suit (Rule 2). Order 28: suits by or against military men, Order 31: suits by or against trustees, executors and administrators (Rule 1: trustee/ executor/ administrator may sue or be sued without joining the persons beneficially interested; Rule 3: the beneficiaries must be joined where the trustee has an interest adverse).

ORDER XXXIV - SUITS RELATING TO MORTGAGES OF IMMOVABLE PROPERTY: Rule 1: PARTIES TO SUITS FOR FORECLOSURE, SALE AND REDEMPTION - subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force, all persons having an interest either in the mortgage-security or in the right of redemption shall be joined as parties to any suit relating to the mortgage (the mortgagee/ mortgagor and persons deriving title from them - all necessary parties); Rule 2: preliminary decree in a foreclosure suit - the court shall pass a preliminary decree (a) ordering that an account be taken of what was due to the plaintiff at the date of such decree for principal and interest on the mortgage, costs of suit and other costs, charges and expenses properly incurred by the mortgagee; (b) directing that, if the defendant pays into court the amount so found due on or before a date within six months from the date on which the court confirms and countersigns the account taken, or such date as the court may fix, the plaintiff shall deliver up all documents in his possession or power relating to the mortgaged property and re-transfer the property; and (c) that if payment is not made on or before such date, the plaintiff shall be entitled to apply for a final decree that the defendant be debarred from all right to redeem the property (foreclosure). Rule 3: final decree in foreclosure suit - upon application by the plaintiff after the expiry of the period; Rule 4: preliminary decree in a suit for sale (similar; the final decree for sale of property or part sufficient to satisfy); Rule 5: final decree in a suit for sale - on application, the court shall pass a final decree directing that the mortgaged property or a sufficient part thereof be sold, and that the proceeds of the sale be applied (a) in payment of the costs of the sale; (b) in payment of what is due to the plaintiff; and (c) the balance (if any) be paid to the defendant or other persons entitled to receive the same. Rule 6: RECOVERY OF BALANCE DUE ON MORTGAGE IN SUIT FOR SALE - where the net proceeds of any sale are insufficient to pay the amount due to the plaintiff, the court may, on application, pass a personal decree against the defendant for the balance (the DEFICIENCY DECREE) provided the balance is legally recoverable from the defendant otherwise than out of the property sold (Sec 90 TPA). Rule 7: preliminary decree in a redemption suit; Rule 8: final decree in a redemption suit - where payment is made, the court shall direct the delivery of documents and re-transfer or, on default, foreclosure or sale; Rule 14: a mortgagee who has obtained a decree for the payment of money in satisfaction of a claim arising under the mortgage shall not be entitled to bring the mortgaged property to sale otherwise than by instituting a suit for sale in enforcement of the mortgage, and he may institute such suit notwithstanding anything contained in Order II Rule 2. Since 1976, the court may order sale in mortgage decrees; the Transfer of Property Act Secs 85-90 and Order 34 operate together; the decrees are preliminary (account of dues; time to pay) and final (foreclosure/ sale). Sale of mortgaged property in the final decree is conducted as in execution (Order 34 Rule 5).

Sec 92: only for public charitable/ religious trusts; breach of trust or directions; the suit must be representative.
Interpleader: plaintiff must be a mere stakeholder claiming no interest other than charges or costs.

Sec 88: no interpleader where a pending suit can decide the rights of all.

sections.title: Alternative Dispute Resolution in the CPC (Sec 89, Order X Rules 1A-1C), Mediation Act 2023 and Pre-Institution Mediation
sections.summary: Sec 89 and Afcons Infrastructure are standard; newer questions test the Mediation Act 2023 and Sec 12A of the Commercial Courts Act.
key_points: Sec 89 - SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES OUTSIDE THE COURT: (1) where it appears to the court that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, the court shall formulate the terms of settlement and give them to the parties for their observations and, after receiving the observations of the parties, the court may reformulate the terms of a possible settlement and refer the same for (a) arbitration; (b) conciliation; (c) judicial settlement including settlement through Lok Adalat; or (d) mediation. (2) where a dispute has been referred (a) for arbitration or conciliation, the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 shall apply as if the proceedings for arbitration or conciliation were referred for settlement under the provisions of that Act; (b) to Lok Adalat, the court shall refer the same to the Lok Adalat in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (1) of Sec 20 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and all other provisions of that Act shall apply in respect of the dispute so referred; (c) for judicial settlement, the court shall refer the same to a suitable institution or person and such institution or person shall be deemed to be a Lok Adalat and all the provisions of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 shall apply as if the dispute were referred to a Lok Adalat under the provisions of that Act; (d) for mediation, the court shall effect a compromise between the parties and shall follow such procedure as may be prescribed.

ORDER X RULES 1A-1C: Rule 1A: after recording the admissions and denials, the court shall direct the parties to the suit to opt either mode of the settlement outside the court as specified in sub-section (1) of Sec 89; on the option of the parties, the court shall fix the date of appearance before such forum or authority as may be opted by the parties. Rule 1B: where a suit is referred to a forum or authority, the parties shall appear before such forum or authority for conciliation of the suit. Rule 1C: where the suit is referred under Rule 1A and the presiding officer of the conciliation forum or authority is satisfied that it would not be proper in the interest of justice to proceed with the matter further, then, it shall refer the matter again to the court and parties shall appear before the court on the date fixed by the court.

SALEM ADVOCATE BAR ASSOCIATION v UNION OF INDIA (2005): the Supreme Court upheld the validity of Sec 89 (and the 2002 amendments) and, to remedy a drafting error, directed that the definitions of 'judicial settlement' and 'mediation' in Sec 89(2) be read as interchanged - i.e., Sec 89(2)(c) and (d) read as: (c) for mediation (the court shall effect a compromise between the parties and follow the procedure prescribed) and (d) for judicial settlement (the court shall refer to a suitable institution or person, deemed to be a Lok Adalat). The Court also framed Model Rules for mediation and directed High Courts to frame rules. AFCONS INFRASTRUCTURE v CHERIAN VARKEY CONSTRUCTION (2010): (1) the court is not required to obtain the consent of parties for referring a case to mediation, conciliation or Lok Adalat - consent is necessary only for ARBITRATION (Sec 89 vs Arbitration Act Sec 7); (2) the court should not apply Sec 89 mechanically; (3) cases normally NOT suitable for ADR: representative suits under Order 1 Rule 8 (public interest); disputes relating to election to public offices; cases involving grant of probate/ letters of administration; cases involving serious and specific allegations of fraud, fabrication of documents, forgery, impersonation, coercion; cases requiring protection of courts (claims against minors, deities and mentally challenged persons); cases involving prosecution for criminal offences; (4) cases normally suitable for ADR: all cases relating to trade, commerce and contracts; all cases arising from strained or broken relationships (family disputes, partition, matrimonial); all cases where there is a need for continuation of the pre-existing relationship (e.g., disputes between landlord and tenant, neighbours, employers/ employees); all cases relating to tortious liability including motor accident claims; all consumer disputes including disputes relating to deficiency of service. Sec 89 reference does not oust the court; if ADR fails, the suit continues.

MEDIATION ACT 2023: enacted in September 2023 (assent 14 September 2023) to promote mediation, including institutional mediation, pre-litigation mediation and online mediation; provides for community mediation, enforceability of mediated settlement agreements (MSA) as if they were a decree/ judgment (Sec 27), registration of MSA with the Mediation Council of India (MCI), time limit of 180 days (extendable by 180 days) for completion of mediation, confidentiality; Sec 5: parties may voluntarily and before filing any suit or proceedings in any court, attempt to settle by pre-litigation mediation; the Act excludes disputes involving prosecution for criminal offences, matters affecting rights of third parties, disputes relating to land acquisition, etc. (First Schedule - disputes not fit for mediation). The Act is being brought into force in phases (verify). COMMERCIAL COURTS ACT 2015, Sec 12A (inserted in 2018): a suit, which does not contemplate any urgent interim relief under the Act, shall not be instituted unless the plaintiff exhausts the remedy of pre-institution mediation in accordance with such manner and procedure as may be prescribed by rules made by the Central Government (Commercial Courts (Pre-Institution Mediation and Settlement) Rules 2018); Patil Automation (P) Ltd v Rakheja Engineers (P) Ltd (2022): Sec 12A is MANDATORY; a suit instituted without pre-institution mediation is liable to be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11 (but prospective from 20 August 2022). The Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and Lok Adalats (award deemed a decree of a civil court, final - Sec 21; no appeal; challenge only by writ). Plea bargaining and arbitration (Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996) complete the framework; settlement through Sec 89 can also be a conciliation under Part III of the Arbitration Act; court-annexed mediation centres.

sections.title: Execution: General Principles, Courts and Section 47 (Secs 36-54)
sections.summary: Execution is consistently among the highest-yield areas. Know which court executes (Secs 37-46), what Sec 47 covers, who is liable (Secs 49-53) and the Supreme Court's 2025-26 timelines.
key_points: EXECUTION = the enforcement of decrees and orders by process of court so as to enable the decree-holder to realise the fruits of the decree. Provisions: Sections 36-74 and Order XXI (the longest Order, with 106 Rules). Sec 36: the provisions of the Code relating to the execution of decrees (including provisions relating to payment under a decree) shall, so far as they are applicable, be deemed to apply to the execution of orders (including payment under an order). Sec 37: 'COURT WHICH PASSED A DECREE' - includes (a) where the decree to be executed has been passed in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction, the court of first instance, and (b) where the court of first instance has ceased to exist or to have jurisdiction to execute it, the court which, if the suit wherein the decree was passed were instituted at the time of making the application for the execution of the decree, would have jurisdiction to try such suit. Sec 38: COURT BY WHICH DECREE MAY BE EXECUTED - a decree may be executed either by the court which passed it, or by the court to which it is sent for execution. Sec 39: TRANSFER OF DECREE FOR EXECUTION - (1) the court which passed a decree may, on the application of the decree-holder, send it for execution to another court, of competent jurisdiction, (a) if the person against whom the decree is passed actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other court; or (b) if such person has not property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the court which passed the decree sufficient to satisfy such decree and has property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other court; or (c) if the decree directs the sale or delivery of immovable property situate outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the court which passed it; or (d) if the court which passed the decree considers for any other reason, which it shall record in writing, that the decree should be executed by such other court. (4) nothing in this section shall be deemed to authorise the court which passed a decree to execute such decree against any person or property outside the local limits of its jurisdiction (2002 amendment - to overcome the earlier practice). Sec 40: transfer of decree to court in another State; Sec 41: result of execution proceedings to be certified by the transferee court; Sec 42: POWERS OF COURT IN EXECUTING TRANSFERRED DECREE - the court executing a decree sent to it shall have the same powers in executing such decree as if it had been passed by itself; Sec 43: execution of decrees passed by Civil Courts in places to which the Code does not extend; Sec 44: execution of decrees passed by Revenue Courts; Sec 44A: reciprocating territories (see 1.4); Sec 45: execution of decrees outside India (the court may send the decree to a court outside India under Central Government order); Sec 46: PRECEPTS - upon the application of the decree-holder the court which passed the decree may, whenever it thinks fit, issue a precept to any other court which would be competent to execute such decree to attach any property belonging to the judgment-debtor and specified in the precept; the court shall proceed to attach the property in the manner prescribed in regard to the attachment of property in execution of a decree; but no attachment under a precept shall continue for more than TWO MONTHS unless the period of attachment is extended by an order of the court which passed the decree or unless before the determination of such attachment the decree has been transferred to the court by which the attachment has been made and the decree-holder has applied to such court for an order for the sale of such property.

Sec 47 - QUESTIONS TO BE DETERMINED BY THE COURT EXECUTING DECREE: (1) all questions arising between the parties to the suit in which the decree was passed, or their representatives, and relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree, shall be determined by the court executing the decree and not by a separate suit. [(2) omitted by the 1976 amendment]. (3) where a question arises as to whether any person is or is not the representative of a party, such question shall, for the purposes of this section, be determined by the court. Explanation I: for the purposes of this section, a plaintiff whose suit has been dismissed and a defendant against whom a suit has been dismissed are parties to the suit. Explanation II: (a) for the purposes of this section, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree shall be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree is passed; and (b) all questions relating to the delivery of possession of such property to such purchaser or his representative shall be deemed to be questions relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree within the meaning of this section. ESSENTIALS: (1) the question must arise between the PARTIES to the suit or their representatives; (2) the question must relate to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree; (3) the question must arise in the execution proceedings. Third parties (not parties) must be dealt with under Order 21 Rules 58 (claims), 97-101 (obstruction) or by separate suits (Order 21 Rule 63). The executing court CANNOT GO BEHIND THE DECREE - it must execute the decree as it stands; it cannot question its correctness or add to or vary it (Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, 1970; Topanmal Chhotamal v Kundomal Gangaram, 1960) - EXCEPTION: where the decree is a NULLITY (passed without inherent jurisdiction, or against a dead person, or violating a statutory prohibition), the executing court can decline execution on that ground (Sunder Dass v Ram Prakash, 1977; Rafique Bibi v Sayed Waliuddin, 2004; Hasham Abbas Sayyad v Usman Abbas Sayyad, 2007). Also: executing court can interpret an ambiguous decree; can determine whether the decree is satisfied; can decide whether the JD's property is attachable; can decide limitation for execution. Sec 47 questions are determined by the executing court even if they involve questions of title between parties (but not those between a decree-holder and a stranger). Sec 47 vs. Order 21 Rule 97-101: in a possession decree, any person (including a stranger) resisting or obstructing is dealt with under Rules 97-103; the question of the right, title and interest are to be determined by that court (Rule 101) - the Supreme Court in Periyammal v V. Rajamani (2025) emphasised these provisions to prevent multiplicity of proceedings.

Sec 49: transferee - every transferee of a decree shall hold the same subject to the equities (if any) which the judgment-debtor might have enforced against the original decree-holder. Sec 50: LEGAL REPRESENTATIVE - (1) where a judgment-debtor dies before the decree has been fully satisfied, the holder of the decree may apply to the court which passed it to execute the same against the legal representative of the deceased. (2) where the decree is executed against such legal representative, he shall be liable only to the extent of the property of the deceased which has come to his hands and has not been duly disposed of; and, for the purpose of ascertaining such liability, the court executing the decree may, of its own motion or on the application of the decree-holder, compel such legal representative to produce such accounts as it thinks fit. Sec 51: POWERS OF COURT TO ENFORCE EXECUTION: subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, the court may, on the application of the decree-holder, order execution of the decree (a) by delivery of any property specifically decreed; (b) by attachment and sale or by the sale without attachment of any property; (c) by arrest and detention in prison for such period not exceeding the period specified in Sec 58, where arrest and detention is permissible under that section; (d) by appointing a receiver; or (e) in such other manner as the nature of the relief granted may require; PROVISO (2002): where the decree is for the payment of money, execution by detention in prison shall not be ordered unless, after giving the judgment-debtor an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be committed to prison, the court, for reasons recorded in writing, is satisfied (a) that the judgment-debtor, with the object or effect of obstructing or delaying the execution of the decree, (i) is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the court, or (ii) has, after the institution of the suit in which the decree was passed, dishonestly transferred, concealed, or removed any part of his property, or committed any other act of bad faith in relation to his property, or (b) that the judgment-debtor has, or has had since the date of the decree, the means to pay the amount of the decree or some substantial part thereof and refuses or neglects or has refused or neglected to pay the same, or (c) that the decree is for a sum for which the judgment-debtor was bound in a fiduciary capacity to account. Explanation: in the calculation of the means of the JD, there shall be left out of account any property which, by or under any law or custom having the force of law for the time being in force, is exempt from attachment in execution of the decree. Sec 52: enforcement of decree against legal representative - where a decree is passed against a party as the legal representative of a deceased person, and the decree is for the payment of money out of the property of the deceased, it may be executed by the attachment and sale of any such property; and if no such property remains in the possession of the JD and he fails to satisfy the court that he has duly applied such property, the decree may be executed against the JD to the extent of the property in respect of which he has failed so to satisfy the court in the same manner as if the decree had been against him personally. Sec 53: liability of ancestral property in hands of son or other descendant - for the purposes of Secs 50 and 52, property in the hands of a son or other descendant which is liable under Hindu law to be attached and sold in execution of a decree against his father, grandfather or great-grandfather, shall be deemed to be property of the deceased which has come to the hands of the son or other descendant as his legal representative. Sec 54: partition of estates or separation of share (execution of decrees for partition of revenue-paying estates by the Collector).

WHO CAN EXECUTE: the decree-holder, his legal representative or transferee (Order 21 Rule 16 - transfer of decree: assignee may apply for execution with notice to the transferor and JD); WHO CAN BE PROCEEDED AGAINST: the judgment-debtor and his legal representative. Joint decree-holders: Order 21 Rule 15 - any one of the joint decree-holders may apply for execution of the whole decree for the benefit of all, if the decree is joint; the court may impose conditions. Execution of a decree against a firm: Order 21 Rule 50. LIMITATION FOR EXECUTION: Art 136 of the Limitation Act 1963 - TWELVE YEARS from the date when the decree or order becomes enforceable (or, where the decree directs payment at a certain date, from that date); for a decree of any civil court (not being a decree granting a mandatory injunction); successive execution applications may be filed within the 12 years; where the decree directs payment at a certain date or on certain conditions, time runs from the date when it becomes enforceable. Sec 48 CPC (the earlier 12-year bar and 'new application after 12 years'), was repealed in 1976. A decree for mandatory injunction: 3 years (Art 135). Execution proceedings are not a suit (Sec 141 CPC applies the CPC provisions to proceedings other than suits as far as possible). Execution proceedings continue as a continuation of the suit (Sec 141). Res judicata applies to execution proceedings (Explanation VII to Sec 11).

RECENT SUPREME COURT DIRECTIONS ON EXECUTION (2025-26): PERIYAMMAL (dead) through LRs v V. RAJAMANI (2025 INSC 329, 6 March 2025): the Supreme Court, alarmed by the pendency of execution petitions, directed all High Courts to ensure that execution petitions already pending (as at March 2025) are disposed of within SIX MONTHS and that all executing courts dispose of execution proceedings within six months of the date of filing, extendable only for reasons recorded in writing; the presiding officer of the executing court is answerable for default; the Supreme Court issued guidelines including that executing courts should not allow withdrawal and refiling of execution petitions without valid reasons (Nov 2025), that the decree-holder be put in possession without delay, and that High Courts collect and submit data on pendency; further directions on monitoring and periodic reporting by the High Courts were issued in later hearings (verify the details). By 2026 the number of pending execution petitions stood at approximately 8 lakh (a reported 7.96 lakh as of April 2026; the Court in 2026 expressed concern that merely seeking figures every six months was inadequate). The Court has repeatedly cited Rahul S. Shah v Jinendra Kumar Gandhi (2021) (guidelines for execution - the executing court to examine the JD on oath regarding assets under Order 21 Rule 41, direct disclosure by affidavit of assets, and dispose of execution within six months) and held that Order 21 Rules 97-101 and Sec 47 together enable the executing court to deal with obstruction by third parties and resolve all issues in one go. These are important 'current affairs' hooks.

sections.title: Modes of Execution, Arrest and Detention, and Attachable Property (Secs 51, 55-61)
sections.summary: The list of property exempt from attachment (Sec 60) and the rules on arrest/ detention (Secs 55-59) are regularly framed as 'which of these cannot be attached?'
key_points: Modes under Sec 51: (a) delivery of property specifically decreed; (b) attachment and sale or sale without attachment; (c) arrest and detention in civil prison; (d) appointment of a receiver; (e) any other manner as the nature of the relief requires (e.g., for a mandatory injunction - Order 21 Rule 32). Order 21 Rule 30: decree for payment of money - execution by detention in prison of the judgment-debtor, or by attachment and sale of his property, or both. Rule 31: decree for specific movable property - by seizure and delivery, or by detention, or attachment, or both; Rule 32: decree for specific performance for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction - (1) where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has wilfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both. (5) where a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the court may, in lieu of or in addition to the above processes, direct that the act required to be done may be done so far as practicable by the decree-holder or some other person appointed by the court, at the cost of the judgment-debtor, and upon the act being done the expenses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the court may direct and may be recovered as if they were included in the decree. Rule 34: decree for execution of document or endorsement of negotiable instrument - where a decree is for the execution of a document or for the endorsement of a negotiable instrument, and the JD neglects or refuses to obey the decree, the decree-holder may prepare a draft of the document or endorsement in accordance with the terms of the decree and deliver the same to the court; the court shall cause the draft to be served on the JD and, on objections, settle the document and execute it. Rule 35: DECREE FOR IMMOVABLE PROPERTY - (1) where a decree is for the delivery of any immovable property, possession thereof shall be delivered to the party to whom it has been adjudged, or to such person as he may appoint to receive delivery on his behalf, and, if necessary, by removing any person bound by the decree who refuses to vacate the property. (2) where a decree is for the joint possession of immovable property, such possession shall be delivered by affixing a copy of the warrant in some conspicuous place on the property and proclaiming, by beat of drum or other customary mode, at some convenient place, the substance of the decree. (3) where possession of any building or enclosure is to be delivered and the person in possession, being bound by the decree, does not afford free access, the court, through its officers, may, after giving reasonable warning and facility to any woman not appearing in public according to the customs of the country to withdraw, remove or open any lock or bolt or break open any door or do any other act necessary for putting the decree-holder in possession. Rule 36: delivery of property in the occupancy of tenant - symbolic possession by affixing the warrant and proclaiming (where the property is in the occupancy of a tenant or other person entitled to occupy and not bound by the decree to relinquish).

ARREST AND DETENTION (Secs 55-59): Sec 55: (1) a judgment-debtor may be arrested in execution of a decree at any hour and in any place, except (a) no arrest shall be made after sunset and before sunrise; (c) no dwelling-house shall be entered after sunset and before sunrise; (d) no outer door of a dwelling-house shall be broken open unless such dwelling-house is in the occupancy of the judgment-debtor and he is not himself present therein, or, being present, refuses or in any way prevents access thereto, but when the officer authorised to make the arrest has duly gained access to any dwelling-house, he may break open the door of any room in which he has reason to believe the JD is to be found; (e) where the room is in the actual occupancy of a woman who is not the JD and who according to the customs of the country does not appear in public, the officer shall give notice to her that she is at liberty to withdraw, and, after allowing a reasonable time for her to withdraw and giving her reasonable facility for withdrawing, may enter the room for the purpose of making the arrest; (f) where the decree in execution of which a JD is arrested is a decree for the payment of money and the JD pays the amount of the decree and the costs of the arrest to the officer arresting him, such officer shall at once release him. (2) where a judgment-debtor is arrested in execution of a money decree and brought before the court, the court shall inform him that he may apply to be declared an insolvent and that he may be discharged if he has not acted in bad faith. Separately, Sec 135 exempts parties, witnesses and pleaders from arrest under civil process while attending court, and Sec 135A exempts members of legislative bodies. Sec 56: PROHIBITION OF ARREST OR DETENTION OF WOMEN IN EXECUTION OF DECREE FOR PAYMENT OF MONEY - notwithstanding anything in this Code, the court shall not order the arrest or detention in the civil prison of a woman in execution of a decree for the payment of money. Sec 57: subsistence allowance - the State Government may fix scales, graded according to the rank, race and nationality of the JD, of monthly allowances payable for the subsistence of JDs; the allowance is payable by the decree-holder. Sec 58 - DETENTION AND RELEASE: (1) every person detained in the civil prison in execution of a decree shall be so detained, (a) where the decree is for the payment of a sum of money exceeding five thousand rupees, for a period up to THREE MONTHS; and (b) where the decree is for the payment of a sum of money exceeding two thousand rupees, but not exceeding five thousand rupees, for a period up to SIX WEEKS: provided that he shall be released from such detention before the expiry of the said period of detention (i) on the amount mentioned in the warrant for his detention being paid to the officer in charge of the civil prison, or (ii) on the decree against him being otherwise fully satisfied, or (iii) on the request of the person at whose instance he has been detained, or (iv) on the omission by the person, at whose instance he has been detained, to pay subsistence allowance, or (v) on the order of the court. (1A) for the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that no order for detention of the JD in civil prison in execution of a decree for the payment of money shall be made where the total amount of the decree does not exceed two thousand rupees. (2) a judgment-debtor released from detention under this section shall not merely by reason of his release be discharged from his debt, but he shall not be liable to be re-arrested under the decree in execution of which he was detained in the civil prison. Sec 59: release on ground of illness - may be released on the ground of serious illness or in case of an infectious disease prevailing in the prison.

SEC 60 - PROPERTY LIABLE TO ATTACHMENT AND SALE IN EXECUTION OF DECREE: (1) the following property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree, namely, lands, houses or other buildings, goods, money, bank-notes, cheques, bills of exchange, hundis, promissory notes, Government securities, bonds or other securities for money, debts, shares in a corporation and, save as hereinafter mentioned, all other saleable property, movable or immovable, belonging to the judgment-debtor, or over which, or the profits of which, he has a disposing power which he may exercise for his own benefit, whether the same be held in the name of the judgment-debtor or by another person in trust for him or on his behalf: PROVIDED THAT THE FOLLOWING PARTICULARS SHALL NOT BE LIABLE TO SUCH ATTACHMENT OR SALE, namely: (a) the necessary wearing apparel, cooking vessels, beds and bedding of the judgment-debtor, his wife and children, and such personal ornaments as, in accordance with religious usage, cannot be parted with by any woman; (b) tools of artisans, and, where the JD is an agriculturist, his implements of husbandry and such cattle and seed-grain as may, in the opinion of the court, be necessary to enable him to earn his livelihood as such, and such portion of agricultural produce or of any class of agricultural produce as may have been declared to be free from liability under the provisions of the next following section; (c) houses and other buildings (with the materials and the sites thereof and the land immediately appurtenant thereto and necessary for their enjoyment) belonging to an agriculturist or a labourer or a domestic servant and occupied by him; (d) books of account; (e) a mere right to sue for damages; (f) any right of personal service; (g) stipends and gratuities allowed to pensioners of the Government or of a local authority or of any other employer, or payable out of any service family pension fund notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government or the State Government in this behalf, and political pensions; (h) the wages of labourers and domestic servants, whether payable in money or in kind; (i) SALARY to the extent of the first one thousand rupees and two-thirds of the remainder in execution of any decree other than one for maintenance (proviso: where any part of such portion of the salary as is liable to attachment has been, for a period of twenty-four months, attached, whether continuously or intermittently, in execution of one and the same decree, such portion shall, for a further period of twelve months, be exempt from attachment); (ia) one-third of the salary in execution of any decree for maintenance; (j) the pay and allowances of persons to whom the Air Force Act 1950, the Army Act 1950, or the Navy Act 1957 applies; (k) all compulsory deposits and other sums in or derived from any fund to which the Provident Funds Act 1925 applies in so far as they are declared by the said Act not to be liable to attachment; (ka) all deposits and other sums in or derived from any fund to which the Public Provident Funds Act 1968 applies in so far as they are declared by the said Act as not to be liable to attachment; (kb) all moneys payable under a policy of insurance on the life of the judgment-debtor; (kc) the interest of a lessee of a residential building to which the provisions of law for the time being in force relating to control of rents and accommodation apply; (l) any allowance forming part of the emoluments of any servant of the Government or of any servant of a railway company or local authority which the appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be exempt from attachment, and any subsistence grant or allowance made to a public officer while under suspension; (m) an expectancy of succession by survivorship or other merely contingent or possible right or interest; (n) a right to future maintenance; (o) any allowance declared by any Indian law to be exempt from liability to attachment or sale in execution of a decree; and (p) where the judgment-debtor is a person liable for the payment of land-revenue, any movable property which, under any law for the time being applicable to him, is exempt from sale for the recovery of an arrear of such revenue. Explanation I: the moneys payable in respect of the allowances mentioned in clauses (g), (h), (i), (ia), (j), (l) and (o) are exempt from attachment or sale, whether before or after they are actually payable, and the liability of such moneys to attachment or sale shall be determined with reference to the character thereof at the time of attachment. Explanation II: in clauses (i) and (ia), 'salary' means the total monthly emoluments, excluding any allowance declared exempt from attachment, derived by a person from his employment whether on duty or on leave. Explanation III: in clauses (j), (l) and (o), 'appropriate Government' means (i) as respects any person in the service of the Central Government, or any servant of a railway administration or of a cantonment authority or of the port authority of a major port, the Central Government; and (ii) as respects any other servant of the Government or a servant of any other local authority, the State Government. Explanation IV: for the purposes of this proviso, wages include wages payable in kind including the portion of agricultural produce payable to the labourers in lieu of their wages. (2) nothing in this section shall be deemed to exempt houses and other buildings (with the materials and the sites thereof and the lands immediately appurtenant thereto and necessary for their enjoyment) from attachment or sale in execution of decrees for rent of any such house, building, site or land.

Sec 61: partial exemption of agricultural produce - the State Government may, by general or special order published in the Official Gazette, declare that such portion of agricultural produce, or of any class of agricultural produce, as may appear to the State Government to be necessary for the purpose of providing for the due cultivation of the land and for the support of the JD and his family until the next harvest, shall, as long as it is in the possession of an agriculturist, be exempt from liability to attachment or sale in execution of a decree. Sec 62: SEIZURE OF MOVABLE PROPERTY IN DWELLING-HOUSE - no person executing any process under this Code directing or authorising seizure of movable property shall enter any dwelling-house after sunset and before sunrise; no outer door shall be broken open unless the house is in the occupancy of the JD and he is not present or refuses access; and the officer shall give due notice to women not appearing in public. Sec 63: property attached in execution of decrees of several courts (the court of the highest grade/ the court that first attached - where property not in custody of any court is attached in execution of decrees of more than one court, the court which shall receive or realise such property and determine claims thereto and objections to the attachment thereof shall be the court of the highest grade, or, where there is no difference in grade between such courts, the court which first attached the property). Sec 64: PRIVATE ALIENATION OF PROPERTY AFTER ATTACHMENT TO BE VOID - (1) where an attachment has been made, any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any interest therein and any payment to the judgment-debtor of any debt, dividend or other moneys contrary to such attachment, shall be void as against all claims enforceable under the attachment. (2) nothing in this section shall apply to any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any interest therein, made in pursuance of any contract for such transfer or delivery entered into and registered before the attachment, or to any payment made in pursuance of any contract entered into and registered before the attachment. Explanation: for the purposes of this section, claims enforceable under an attachment include claims for the rateable distribution of assets. The alienation is void only against the attaching decree-holder (and others claiming rateable distribution); it is valid between the parties (Sec 64 is relative).

rows: Exceeding Rs 2,000 but not exceeding Rs 5,000

common_traps: Salary: the first Rs 1,000 and two-thirds of the remainder are exempt in execution of ordinary money decrees (clause (i)); in execution of maintenance decrees one-third of the salary is exempt (clause (ia)).
Houses of agriculturist/ labourer/ domestic servant occupied by him are exempt, but not for decrees for rent of such house (Sec 60(2)).
Women cannot be arrested/ detained for money decrees (Sec 56).

Life insurance money payable on JD's life is exempt; a mere right to sue for damages is not attachable; books of account are exempt.
